<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **step-fixed-setup-framework** [claim](#stmt-lem-fw-uniform) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-fw-uniform): Contradiction with the upper exponent in a single fixed setup. -> Uniform small-scale exponent bounds with explicit dependence on fixed setup bounds.
- **step-energy-extraction-closure** [claim](#stmt-lem-fw-closure) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-fw-closure): Orthogonal row-energy control, coherent finite extraction and successive extrema on feasible closed slices. -> Legitimate finite approximating experiments for extremal growth and minimal costs.
- **step-probability-comparisons** [claim](#stmt-lem-fw-information) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-fw-information): Capacity counting, likelihood ratios and conditional information chain rules. -> Score stability and precisely qualified information stability under restriction.
- **step-cylinder-locality-tests** [claim](#stmt-cyl-polynomial-tests) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cyl-polynomial-tests): Gaussian frame kernels, symmetries, phase-density bounds and polynomial sublevel estimates. -> Uniform locality and finite parameter ranges for cylinder tests.
- **step-cylinder-saturation** [claim](#stmt-cyl-split-saturation) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cyl-split-saturation): One-time control, regularity peeling, prefix and tail exponent comparisons and minimality. -> Saturated intermediate energy and regularity benchmarks.
- **step-matched-chains-and-groups** [claim](#stmt-cyl-matched-chain) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cyl-intersection-2): Two-shear overlap bounds, removal of incompatible rows, common charts and backward gate construction followed by forward regularization. -> Compatible documented gates and extractable near-extremal groups.
- **step-cylinder-planck-and-affine** [claim](#stmt-cyl-affine) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cyl-affine): Classical comparison at sub-Planck endings, compact width-profile extraction, minimal-cost improvement and normalization near differentiability points. -> Affine extremal configurations with compatible shears and preserved minimal costs.
- **step-causal-row-laws** [claim](#stmt-cyl-phase-name) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cyl-phase-name): Necessary-predecessor rarity, measurable completion events, forward score flattening and uniform finite prediction lists. -> Measurable conditional row profiles, causal time uncertainty and phase-name scores.
- **step-lower-dimensional-wave-bounds** [claim](#stmt-low-scalar) / [proof](#proof-stmt-low-scalar): Hilbert-valued wave-envelope extension, parabolic kinetic reduction, collision estimates and masked scalar-channel induction. -> Kinetic and scalar estimates with finite-mask subpower losses.
- **step-angular-memory-hybrid-zero** [claim](#stmt-low-hybrid-zero) / [proof](#proof-stmt-low-hybrid-zero): Scalar-channel memory and a stopping-scale split into transverse and nearby velocity contributions. -> Exclusion of a strictly nonclassical positive zero-cost configuration.
- **step-planar-incidence-bootstrap** [claim](#stmt-low-conditional-incidence) / [proof](#proof-stmt-low-conditional-incidence): Probability sampling for the discretized Furstenberg theorem and alternating point-line score bootstraps. -> Finite-query conditional incidence score gain.
- **step-classical-zero-cost-exclusion** [claim](#stmt-low-classical-zero-cost) / [proof](#proof-stmt-low-classical-zero-cost): Boosted name profiles, plane avoidance, transverse conditional pins, finite Ramsey selection and planar incidence recovery. -> Classical positive extremizers cannot have both shear costs zero.
- **step-canonical-names-and-traces** [claim](#stmt-names-memory) / [proof](#proof-stmt-names-memory): Shear-difference Taylor comparisons, regularity lower bounds, endpoint recovery, monotone angular traces and mixed coefficient traces. -> Nonnegative canonical excess with endpoint equality and quantitative angular memory.
- **step-common-phase-replicas** [claim](#stmt-names-walks) / [proof](#proof-stmt-names-walks): Admissible side conditioning, representative common phase, causal mark dimension, cost-improvement separation and stationary fiber resampling. -> Finite conditional replica and walk laws with explicit information budgets and phase increment identities.
- **step-score-and-projection-calculus** [claim](#stmt-names-projection-rule) / [proof](#proof-stmt-names-projection-rule): Joint score subsequences, monotone triangular traces, future-prefix identities, controlled changes of law and record-specific projection lists. -> Conditional projection lower bounds valid for actual finite-name score tests.
- **step-radial-and-pin-products** [claim](#stmt-names-radial-pin-product) / [proof](#proof-stmt-names-radial-pin-product): Finite radial exclusion, joining-tube rate dichotomy, parent-centered direction transfer and low-tube pin-product analysis. -> High radial direction bounds and a local low-exponent product substitute.
- **step-local-phase-rate-inequalities** [claim](#stmt-int-orientation-rates) / [proof](#proof-stmt-int-orientation-rates): Contact-reading recovery, angular and commutator modes, projection amplification, many-leg walks and mark motions. -> Time, width, orientation and residual phase-rate bounds for admissible tangent data.
- **step-interior-actions** [claim](#stmt-int-actions) / [proof](#proof-stmt-int-actions): Horizontal-width and binary-layer lower bounds followed by finite linear-inequality combinations. -> Branch-specific freezing and moving directions with positive excess surplus.
- **step-cylinder-boundary-and-path-closure** [claim](#stmt-thm-cylinder) / [proof](#proof-stmt-act-off-gap-path-2): Fixed-width line tests, stationary and strict boundary applications, finite off-gap motion and exhaustive affine-case path contradictions. -> Classical cylinder bound followed by the hybrid bound with its strict comparison justified.
- **step-round-locality-saturation** [claim](#stmt-rt-saturation) / [proof](#proof-stmt-rt-saturation): Round packet kernels, enlarged-test covering, single-time control, regularity peeling and sharp composition across free gaps. -> Finite free exponent and legitimate outer-closure saturation at inserted round cuts.
- **step-thin-round-transfer** [claim](#stmt-rt-thin-exclusion) / [proof](#proof-stmt-rt-classical-base-2): Thin predecessor grouping, conformal flattening, exact wave transport, cell-capacity allocation, weight comparison and classicalization of the base. -> Thin saturated round endings obey the cylinder exponent bounds.
- **step-round-uncertainty-and-slabs** [claim](#stmt-lem-rt-slab-removal) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-rt-slab-removal): Classical test-volume bounds, angular uncertainty saturation, spatial readout and separate tiny-cap and transverse slab estimates. -> Round labels at the required uncertainty scale and conditional velocity laws without planar concentration.
- **step-round-profiles-and-outgoing** [claim](#stmt-prop-rt-outgoing) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-rt-outgoing): Forward selected laws, ancestor stability, deterministic profiles, time spread, interval differentiation, dyadic stationarity and transverse pin incidence. -> Outgoing depth entropy and the wave width derivative bound on valid measuring laws.
- **step-round-descent-closure** [claim](#stmt-thm-round) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-rt-descent-2): Classical integration and a monotone-threshold moving-or-vertical descent for wave excess. -> The classical round bound and then the wave round bound, including finite contraction stacks.
- **step-physical-input-and-synthesis** [claim](#stmt-prop-phys-annular) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-phys-synthesis-2): Null-coordinate identification, uniform initial-slice packet localization, predecessor volumes, full input regularity, terminal synthesis and amplitude decomposition. -> Uniform annular physical smoothing with arbitrary positive loss.
- **step-frequency-summation-and-interpolation** [claim](#stmt-cor-full-range) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-full-range): Summable Sobolev annular factors, low-frequency kernel estimates and interpolation with energy and annular supremum bounds. -> Critical smoothing and the full strict Euclidean positive-regularity range.
- **step-maximal-wave-and-fourier-summation** [claim](#stmt-cor-br-nonmaximal) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-br-nonmaximal): Established maximal implications, time Sobolev embedding, smooth-factor transfer, density, fixed-radius interpolation and duality. -> Maximal half-wave convergence and maximal and individual Bochner–Riesz bounds in their separate strict ranges.

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **invariant-positive-sobolev-loss**: The critical Euclidean spacetime estimate allows every positive Sobolev loss, with a constant depending on that loss.
- **invariant-fixed-setup-before-scale-limit**: Structural bounds and the branch operation bound remain fixed during each inner scale limit; uniform estimates may depend on those bounds.
- **invariant-restriction-information-budget**: Restrictions of probability bounded below preserve negligible normalized conditional information. Exponent-zero probability alone does not supply this conclusion.
- **invariant-row-energy-versus-copies**: Disjoint analyzed row restrictions obey the summed energy bound. Separate evolved copies require the separate copy bound.
- **invariant-finite-round-operator-stacks**: The round-cone exponent bounds permit a fixed finite list of admissible row contractions and arbitrary separable Hilbert multiplicity under the model's support and error conventions.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-lossless-endpoint**: Treat the critical estimate as a lossless spacetime bound. -> The conclusion requires positive Sobolev loss and supplies no lossless endpoint estimate or limiting control of its constants.
- **anti-unbounded-inner-setup**: Increase cutoff powers or operator-stack size while taking the inner scale limit. -> The uniform bound applies within a fixed setup and does not provide uniform constants across increasing setup bounds.
- **anti-rare-event-information-transfer**: Reuse an auxiliary information budget after an arbitrary restriction of exponent-zero probability. -> The information preservation assertion requires a probability lower bound; score stability alone does not establish preservation of the information budget.
- **anti-copied-energy-orthogonality**: Charge all descendant interval inputs to an orthogonal partition of the original energy. -> Time subdivision copies the input. The summed energy bound for disjoint row projections does not apply to separate copies.
- **anti-quantum-ancestral-sampling**: Interpret packet reachability as a sampled classical ancestral trajectory through hybrid masks. -> Geometric predecessor inclusions support locality estimates without providing a joint ancestral probability law.
- **anti-maximal-range-from-fixed-radius-duality**: Extend the maximal Bochner–Riesz conclusion throughout the fixed-radius range by interpolation and duality. -> The nonmaximal argument applies to individual linear means; its broader range does not establish the corresponding maximal bound.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `not_applicable`. The principal result is a continuous Euclidean half-wave estimate quantified over Schwartz inputs and every positive Sobolev loss, rather than a finite constructive computation. Its cylinder and round-cone reductions use limiting exponent data, subsequence extraction, and entropy contradictions. The source explicitly states: "These lemmas assert neither an exactly extremizing input nor an infinite chain of operators." Finite tests of an elementary allocation or probability lemma would certify only that restricted auxiliary construction and would not decide the analytic estimate or its scale limits.

## 5. Domain engineering contracts

| domain | applies | strength | maturity | basis | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| software | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The half-wave estimates specify continuous operator bounds. A software interface, discretization, and error contract for evaluating these operators are ABSENT. |
| games_simulation | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The evolution studied is a free Euclidean wave. The paper supplies no construction for collision handling, boundary reflections, or nonlinear simulation updates. |
| tools | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The uniform exponent bound requires a fixed admissible setup and uniform tail hypotheses. It does not construct an executable checker for those hypotheses or compute a usable scale threshold. |
| algorithms | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | The cell-capacity lemma gives an explicit finite allocation procedure: remove excess target assignments proportionally, then distribute retained mass among neighboring source cells according to their energies. This construction preserves source capacities and controls each label's loss. |
| data_structures | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Canonical names are finite mathematical records with proved refinement lists. The paper does not construct a storage or indexing structure with operational bounds for maintaining these records. |
| hardware_accelerators | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The Hilbert-valued wave-envelope extension makes its analytic constant independent of the Hilbert space. This does not specify a parallel kernel, memory layout, or accelerator execution model. |
| crypto_security | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The conditional information lemma concerns surprise tails and preservation of information budgets under positive-probability restrictions. It supplies no cryptographic construction or adversarial security definition. |
| machine_learning | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Conditional replica sampling is an auxiliary proof construction using specified probability kernels. The paper gives no learned model, training procedure, or method for estimating those kernels from data. |
| optimisation_operations_research | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | Finite cell-capacity transfer provides a feasible fractional allocation under neighborhood and overlap constraints. It can be adapted to capacity redistribution when proportional removal and the stated multiplicative loss are acceptable; no optimality conclusion is supplied. |
| distributed_systems | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The energy lemma distinguishes disjoint restrictions from separate copies of a state. It gives no protocol for replicas communicating under failures, delays, or concurrent updates. |
| other | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The Bochner–Riesz conclusions concern continuous Fourier summation and analytic convergence. A finite filtering implementation with approximation errors and a computational resource contract is ABSENT. |

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **limit-positive-loss-endpoint** (edge_case): The critical estimate permits a fixed positive Sobolev loss. The lossless endpoint and uniform control of the constant as the loss vanishes are not established. Blocked use: ['Removing the Sobolev multiplier from the critical estimate.', 'Claiming a quantitative limiting behavior for the loss-dependent constant.']
- **limit-euclidean-propagator** (formal_scope): The main estimate concerns the specified Euclidean half-wave. A corresponding estimate for variable coefficients, boundary reflections, or nonlinear evolution requires a separate result. Blocked use: ['Applying the theorem directly to a wave equation on a general manifold.', 'Treating the estimate as a stability theorem for nonlinear or bounded-domain simulations.']
- **limit-fixed-inner-setup** (hypothesis): Structural bounds, cutoff powers, and branch operation counts must remain fixed during each inner scale limit. Uniform constants may depend on the chosen setup. Blocked use: ['Increasing the number of masks with the inner scale.', 'Claiming uniform bounds across an outer family whose setup parameters grow without bound.']
- **limit-ordered-tangent-errors** (approximation): Positive gaps and finite query lists are fixed before inner limits. Errors must be made small relative to a gap before that gap shrinks. Blocked use: ['Dividing an uncontrolled vanishing error by a shrinking gap.', 'Interchanging mesh refinement and scale limits without the prescribed accuracy control.']
- **limit-relative-energy-tails** (approximation): Negligibility relative to the original energy does not automatically imply negligibility relative to an arbitrarily small subexperiment energy. Blocked use: ['Normalizing a tiny-energy component using the original tail hypothesis alone.', "Applying a uniform model exponent before verifying the selected component's own admissibility."]
- **limit-copy-energy-accounting** (hypothesis): Summable energy bounds for orthogonal analyzed-row restrictions do not apply to separate evolved copies of the input. Blocked use: ['Charging all descendant time-interval inputs to a disjoint partition of the original energy.', 'Inferring orthogonality of synthesized states from disjoint analyzed rows.']
- **limit-closure-attainment** (nonconstructive): Extremal data are attained only under the stated compactness or bounded optimizing-sequence hypotheses. Feasibility and boundedness must be established again when a coordinate is added. Blocked use: ['Minimizing a new shear cost using only compactness of previously selected coordinates.', 'Claiming an explicit exactly extremizing input from the closure construction.']
- **limit-admissible-extraction** (hypothesis): Finite-class and group extraction preserve the model exponent only when the selected experiments satisfy fixed-setup admissibility, overlap, locality, and energy requirements. Blocked use: ["Using a formal maximizing class that fails the model's density or tail conditions.", 'Applying group extraction with uncontrolled label overlap.']
- **limit-information-under-restriction** (hypothesis): A restriction of exponent-zero probability does not by itself preserve a negligible conditional mutual-information budget. Deterministic score stability and information stability have different hypotheses. Blocked use: ['Reusing an auxiliary information budget after an arbitrary subpower restriction.', 'Replacing a positive probability lower bound by exponent-zero probability without a new estimate.']
- **limit-quantum-predecessor-laws** (formal_scope): Packet reachability provides geometric predecessor inclusions for locality estimates. It does not supply a classical ancestral probability coupling through hybrid masks. Blocked use: ['Sampling a hybrid output packet together with a purported classical ancestral trajectory.', "Imposing the original intermediate state's support after a new input restriction that may undo cancellation."]
- **limit-measurable-restriction-law** (hypothesis): Pre-synthesis restrictions require measurable versions under the full analyzed row-energy law. Assigned laws suffice only at terminal readout, and newly formed laws may require new versions. Blocked use: ['Choosing a pre-synthesis mask solely from null-set equivalence under a fractional assigned law.', 'Reusing old measurable versions under a new undominated row law without verification.']
- **limit-hybrid-name-domain** (hypothesis): Hybrid canonical entropy comparisons require the stated normal-width slack and enlargement restriction. Endpoint statements use the specified continuity argument. Blocked use: ['Applying hybrid canonical nonnegativity at arbitrary normal resolutions.', 'Claiming endpoint recovery at points outside the listed equality and prediction regimes.']
- **limit-spreading-and-crossing** (hypothesis): Interior action inequalities require their branch-specific angular positivity, radial spreading, crossing, and line-avoidance hypotheses, except for the explicitly stated exceptions. Blocked use: ['Assigning radial spreading to an artificial quadratic branch merely from matching coordinates.', 'Using a linear motion action outside its angular-rate range.', 'Using a quadratic line-avoidance conclusion for a general exact side at unit cost.']
- **limit-strict-boundary-memory** (hypothesis): The strict affine boundary derivative bounds depend on the required positive boundary prefix-memory slope. The curvature conditions alone do not imply those bounds. Blocked use: ['Dropping the boundary memory hypothesis from the strict affine boundary result.']
- **limit-projection-record-budget** (hypothesis): The conditional projection rule requires source and direction mass bounds, control of source-record information, and output lists indexed by the full record. Rare-event use requires the stronger stated information scaling. Blocked use: ['Replacing the full record by its direction when different records carry different output lists.', 'Applying the projection rule after a rare restriction using only the original negligible normalized information bound.']
- **limit-thin-wave-transfer** (approximation): Thin-round transfer needs buffered conformal charts, packet association estimates, uncertainty-compatible weights, and the prescribed order of comparison precisions. The normal quantum evolution is retained in its stated regime. Blocked use: ['Inferring transformed energy bounds from conformal covariance alone.', 'Replacing the normal propagator by classical rays throughout the normal quantum range.', 'Choosing integration orders before controlling their derivative costs and the fixed support bounds.']
- **limit-capacity-transfer-preconditions** (hypothesis): Finite assignment transfer requires nonnegative energies and errors, the target-capacity inequalities, bounded source overlap, and assignments fitting each target energy. Blocked use: ['Transferring assignments when the neighborhood capacity inequality fails.', 'Treating fractional feasibility as an integral allocation or optimality theorem.']
- **limit-capacity-error-removal** (edge_case): Excess assignments are removed proportionally within each target cell. The permitted error is charged to that cell rather than independently to every label. Blocked use: ['Multiplying the allowed discarded mass by the number of labels in a cell.', 'Retaining positive assignments from a cell with no neighboring source energy after excess removal.']
- **limit-capacity-overlap-divisor** (hypothesis): The proportional source allocation includes both capacity and overlap divisors. Aggregation preserves the resulting retained label mass without an additional loss. Blocked use: ['Omitting the overlap divisor when a source cell belongs to several target neighborhoods.', 'Claiming a smaller loss factor without an independent allocation argument.']
- **limit-physical-annular-input** (hypothesis): The physical annular estimate assumes the specified smooth frequency support and uniform rescaled derivative bounds. Input regularity and terminal synthesis are separate obligations. Blocked use: ['Applying the annular bound to arbitrary rough multipliers.', 'Skipping initial-slice regularity because the null-coordinate evolution has the right cone phase.', 'Using terminal synthesis without its plateau and dyadic partition conditions.']
- **limit-maximal-versus-spacetime** (hypothesis): Maximal half-wave convergence requires the stronger stated Sobolev regularity. The spacetime estimate with arbitrary positive loss does not alone give the same maximal conclusion. Blocked use: ['Replacing the maximal regularity threshold by the critical spacetime threshold.']
- **limit-maximal-versus-fixed-radius** (formal_scope): Fixed-radius Bochner–Riesz interpolation and duality do not extend the maximal theorem throughout the nonmaximal range. Both conclusions retain their strict order conditions. Blocked use: ['Inferring maximal boundedness throughout the fixed-radius exponent range.', 'Including the critical summation order by continuity without an endpoint argument.']
- **limit-finite-certification-scope** (nonconstructive): Finite tests of cell allocation can check that auxiliary construction. They cannot decide the continuous smoothing theorem or certify its subsequence and scale-limit arguments. Blocked use: ['Presenting agreement on finite examples as certification of the main analytic theorem.', 'Treating the limiting profile argument as an executable solver with a proved resource bound.']

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We prove the critical <i>L</i><sup>3</sup> local smoothing estimate for the wave equation in three spatial dimensions, with every positive Sobolev loss. This resolves Sogge's Euclidean local smoothing conjecture in dimension three.

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
### Introduction

Let $$\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx,
 \qquad
 Uf(x,t)=\frac1{(2\pi)^3}
       \int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{i(x\cdot\xi+t|\xi|)}\widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi.$$ For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, write $J^\alpha=(1-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}$, with Fourier multiplier $(1+|\xi|^2)^{\alpha/2}$. For $p>2$, the sharp fixed-time $L^p$ estimate has Sobolev loss $2(1/2-1/p)$ in three dimensions (Peral 1980; Miyachi 1980) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[Peral1980](#ref-Peral1980), [Miyachi1980](#ref-Miyachi1980)]. Time integration can recover part of that loss. Sogge’s Euclidean local smoothing conjecture (Sogge 1991) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[Sogge1991](#ref-Sogge1991)] predicts, for $2<p<\infty$, the strict range $\alpha>\max\{0,1-3/p\}$; its critical exponent is $p=3$. Our main result treats that exponent.

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1** (Critical local smoothing). *For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $C_\varepsilon<\infty$ such that <a id="eq:intro-main"></a>$$\label{eq:intro-main}
 \lVert Uf\rVert_{L^3(\mathbb R^3\times[1,2])}
 \le C_\varepsilon\lVert J^\varepsilon f\rVert_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)}
 \qquad (f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)).$$*

</div>

<a id="eq:intro-full"></a>
The critical estimate supplies the interpolation point for the full Euclidean range: the $L^2$ energy estimate gives the exponents below $p=3$, and an annular $L^\infty$ kernel bound gives those above it. Frequency summation then yields Corollary <a href="#cor:full-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:full-range">125</a>: $$\label{eq:intro-full}
 \lVert Uf\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3\times[1,2])}
 \le C_{p,\alpha}\lVert J^\alpha f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)},
 \qquad
 2<p<\infty,\quad \alpha>\max\{0,1-3/p\}.$$ Together, these estimates resolve Sogge’s Euclidean local smoothing conjecture in three spatial dimensions. At $p=3$, the estimate holds with every positive Sobolev loss; the lossless estimate $\varepsilon=0$ is not addressed.

There is also a pointwise consequence for the wave evolution. Define the finite-time maximal half-wave by $U_*f(x)=\sup_{0<t<1}|Uf(x,t)|$. For $3\le p<\infty$ and $s>1-2/p$, Corollary <a href="#cor:wave-maximal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:wave-maximal">126</a> gives $\lVert U_*f\rVert_p\le C_{p,s}\lVert J^s f\rVert_p$ and almost-everywhere convergence $Uf(x,t)\to f(x)$ as $t\downarrow0$ for data with $J^s f\in L^p$. The established implication from local smoothing uses Sobolev embedding in time. Its extra cost explains the stronger regularity hypothesis: at $p=3$, spacetime smoothing allows every positive loss, whereas this maximal conclusion requires $s>1/3$.

<a id="eq:intro-br-means"></a>
The local-smoothing estimate also has a consequence for Fourier summation. For $R>0$, $\delta>0$, and $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, define the Bochner–Riesz means and their maximal operator by $$\label{eq:intro-br-means}
 \begin{split}
 B_R^\delta f(x)
 &=\frac1{(2\pi)^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{ix\cdot\xi}
       \left(1-\frac{|\xi|^2}{R^2}\right)_+^\delta
       \widehat f(\xi)\,d\xi,\\
 B_*^\delta f(x)&=\sup_{R>0}|B_R^\delta f(x)|.
 \end{split}$$ Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 of Beltran–Hickman–Sogge (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2019) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey)] turn local smoothing into Bochner–Riesz estimates. Section <a href="#sec:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:bochner-riesz">11</a> applies them to <a href="#eq:intro-full" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:intro-full">[eq:intro-full]</a>: Theorem <a href="#thm:br-maximal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:br-maximal">127</a> bounds $B_*^\delta$ strongly on $L^p$ and gives $B_R^\delta f\to f$ almost everywhere for $3\le p<\infty$ and $\delta>1-3/p$. Separately, Corollary <a href="#cor:br-nonmaximal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:br-nonmaximal">128</a> gives uniform bounds for the individual means throughout the strict range $\delta>\max\{3|1/p-1/2|-1/2,0\}$, $1\le p\le\infty$. The individual bounds control Fourier summation uniformly in its radius. The stronger maximal bound controls all radii simultaneously and makes convergence stable under $L^p$ approximation; this is what permits almost-everywhere recovery of arbitrary $L^p$ data. Here the strict condition on the summation order absorbs the positive loss in local smoothing, so no Sobolev regularity of the input is required.

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### History and significance

Sogge introduced local smoothing in his study of circular maximal operators and their variable-coefficient analogues (Sogge 1991) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[Sogge1991](#ref-Sogge1991)]. He proved a positive gain from time averaging in two spatial dimensions and proposed the critical higher-dimensional formulation in (Sogge 1991, sec. 4, especially (4.5)) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[Sogge1991](#ref-Sogge1991)]. The conjecture measures the improvement over the sharp fixed-time estimates of Peral and Miyachi (Peral 1980; Miyachi 1980) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[Peral1980](#ref-Peral1980), [Miyachi1980](#ref-Miyachi1980)]. In three dimensions it asks to recover almost $1/p$ derivatives when $p\ge3$; at $p=3$, time averaging should remove all but an arbitrarily small part of the fixed-time loss of $1/3$. The connection with Fourier summation was already part of this formulation: Sogge showed how critical smoothing implies Bochner–Riesz bounds.

One approach separates the angular decomposition of the wave from the geometry of its rays. Mockenhaupt–Seeger–Sogge developed square-function estimates and their relation to local smoothing, including a framework for Fourier integral operators satisfying cinematic curvature (Mockenhaupt, Seeger, and Sogge 1992, 1993) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[MockenhauptSeegerSogge1992](#ref-MockenhauptSeegerSogge1992), [MockenhauptSeegerSogge1993](#ref-MockenhauptSeegerSogge1993)]. A square function sums the squared magnitudes of the angular pieces at each spacetime point before taking a norm. It therefore retains information about where those pieces overlap. Geometric estimates for thin tubes enter when this overlap is related to the initial data. This approach gave partial smoothing gains and remained important near the critical exponent.

Wolff obtained the conjectured gain for large $p$ in two spatial dimensions by wave-packet localization and induction on scales (Wolff 2000) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[Wolff2000](#ref-Wolff2000)]. His decoupling approach estimates the sum of angular pieces using their separate $L^p$ norms. Łaba–Wolff extended this method to higher dimensions (Łaba and Wolff 2002) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[LabaWolff2002](#ref-LabaWolff2002)], and Garrigós–Seeger combined the induction scheme with bilinear restriction estimates to improve cone plate-decomposition inequalities (Garrigós and Seeger 2009) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[GarrigosSeeger2009](#ref-GarrigosSeeger2009)]. These results distinguished sharp derivative gain from the full conjectured range of exponents. Bourgain–Demeter then proved sharp cone decoupling in every dimension (Bourgain and Demeter 2015, Theorem 1.2) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[BourgainDemeter2015](#ref-BourgainDemeter2015)]. Its local-smoothing consequence gives the conjectured gain for $p\ge4$ in three spatial dimensions, leaving the critical $p=3$ estimate beyond that range.

Beltran–Hickman–Sogge extended the decoupling method to variable coefficients and proved sharp smoothing gains for wave equations on compact Riemannian manifolds and a broader class of Fourier integral operators (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2020) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2020](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2020)]. The geometric obstruction depends on the setting. Minicozzi–Sogge constructed metrics with concentrating families of geodesics (Minicozzi and Sogge 1997) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[MinicozziSogge1997](#ref-MinicozziSogge1997)]; in spatial dimension three these examples require $p\ge10/3$ for the full smoothing gain on general manifolds (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2020, sec. 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2020](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2020)]. For the broader cinematic-curvature class, the $p\ge4$ range proved by Beltran–Hickman–Sogge is sharp in dimension three (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2020, Theorem 1.2 and Proposition 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2020](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2020)]. These distinctions explain the Euclidean qualification in the conjecture considered here. In the broader setting of uniformly elliptic, time-independent wave equations with real coefficients of bounded $C^{1,1}$ norm, Rozendaal–Schippa obtain a diagonal $p=3$ estimate for $\alpha>2/9$ (Rozendaal and Schippa 2026, Corollary 1.2) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[RozendaalSchippa2026](#ref-RozendaalSchippa2026)].

The two-dimensional completion illustrates the importance of retaining spatial overlap information. There Bourgain–Demeter’s theorem gives the full smoothing gain for $p\ge6$; Guth–Wang–Zhang reached the critical exponent $p=4$ through a sharp cone square-function estimate (Guth, Wang, and Zhang 2020) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[GuthWangZhang2020](#ref-GuthWangZhang2020)]. Their stronger wave-envelope estimate tracks how packets occupy regions at intermediate angular scales and exploits sparse packet configurations. This has a direct role in the present proof: we use the wave-envelope theorem as a lower-dimensional input, while the three-dimensional argument must control the additional direction and the changes of geometry between scales.

A further route uses transverse interactions between wave packets. The multilinear estimates of Bennett–Carbery–Tao and the multilinear-to-linear reduction of Bourgain–Guth (Bennett, Carbery, and Tao 2006; Bourgain and Guth 2011) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[BennettCarberyTao2006](#ref-BennettCarberyTao2006), [BourgainGuth2011](#ref-BourgainGuth2011)] lead to a broad–narrow strategy: separate contributions from many distinct directions from those concentrated near a lower-dimensional direction space. Guth’s polynomial-partitioning method provides a weaker $k$-broad estimate for the former, while the latter requires rescaling and induction (Guth 2018) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[Guth2018](#ref-Guth2018)]. Ou–Wang adapt this architecture to the cone, combining broad estimates with narrow decoupling and Lorentz rescaling (Ou and Wang 2022) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[OuWang2022](#ref-OuWang2022)].

Gao–Liu–Miao–Xi use this broad–narrow architecture for local smoothing. Rescaling changes the class of phases to be controlled; their argument treats general positively curved cones and combines broad estimates with narrow decoupling in scale-dependent phase classes (Gao et al. 2023) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[GaoLiuMiaoXi2023](#ref-GaoLiuMiaoXi2023)]. In three spatial dimensions they obtain, at $p=3$, every Sobolev exponent $\alpha>1/9$, or equivalently a smoothing gain below $2/9$ (Gao et al. 2023, Corollary 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[GaoLiuMiaoXi2023](#ref-GaoLiuMiaoXi2023)].

Gan–He–Li–Wu combine refined decoupling with estimates for the local $L^2$ energy and incidence geometry of wave packets (Gan et al. 2026) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[GanHeLiWu2026](#ref-GanHeLiWu2026)]. Their packet density measures energy in windows compatible with Lorentz rescaling. A simultaneous broad and two-ends reduction retains transverse contributions and controls concentration in short portions of packets; in dimension three, slab coverings sharpen the energy and incidence estimates together. Theorem 1.3 of their January 2026 version gives the conjectured gain for $p\ge10/3$, but does not include $p=3$. Interpolation of the $p=10/3$ estimate with the $L^2$ energy bound gives $\alpha>1/12$ at $p=3$, improving the preceding $1/9$ threshold. The remaining fixed positive loss is the gap addressed by Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.

Our proof also studies packet concentration across scales, but its central quantity is the entropy of a finite phase-space record. The records retain the changing shear frames as well as the time and direction information. The proof uses two external quantitative inputs: the planar Furstenberg theorem of Ren–Wang (Ren and Wang 2025, Theorem 4.1) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[RenWang2025](#ref-RenWang2025)] and the cone wave-envelope theorem of Guth–Wang–Zhang (Guth, Wang, and Zhang 2020, Theorem 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[GuthWangZhang2020](#ref-GuthWangZhang2020)]. The former follows a line of discretized incidence and projection work including Katz–Tao, Orponen–Shmerkin, and Shmerkin–Wang (Katz and Tao 2001; Orponen and Shmerkin 2023; Shmerkin and Wang 2025) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[KatzTao2001](#ref-KatzTao2001), [OrponenShmerkin2023](#ref-OrponenShmerkin2023), [ShmerkinWang2025](#ref-ShmerkinWang2025)]. Section <a href="#sec:low" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:low">4</a> states these inputs and proves the specialized probabilistic and Hilbert-valued consequences used below. The extremal reductions and entropy inequalities then connect this lower-dimensional information to the three-dimensional wave estimate.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Structure of the argument

We first seek the estimate on one frequency annulus $|\xi|\asymp H^{-1}$: the physical half-wave should map $L^3$ into spacetime $L^3$ with a loss of at most $H^{-\delta}$ for every $\delta>0$. Summing these estimates gives Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>. On a fixed angular chart, null coordinates turn the light rays into rays with velocities $(A,|A|^2)$, $A\in\mathbb R^2$. We analyze the wave into packets and measure their energy by squared $L^2$ norms.

At the terminal time length $H$, the packet positions have width $H$ and their angular aperture has size one. Write $m_{j,Q}$ for the packet energy assigned to a spatial $H$-cube $Q$ at the start of the $j$th time interval. The synthesis estimate <a href="#eq:phys-synthesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-synthesis">[eq:phys-synthesis]</a> controls the physical cubed $L^3$ norm by $H^{-1/2}\sum_{j,Q}m_{j,Q}^{3/2}$, with an arbitrarily small power loss and a negligible error. Thus the main task is to bound a cubic sum of packet masses. Energy is copied by evolution into descendant time intervals; those descendants are not orthogonal pieces of the original input.

The intermediate scales require more flexible position and direction windows. For the round model $(A,|A|^2)$, a window of angular radius $r$ has position widths $\ell r$ and $\ell r^2$ at time length $\ell$; a parameter $f\le1$ measures its relative thickness near a hyperquadric. Thin round windows lead to the cylinder $(X,X^2,N)$. There $r$ controls the curved base direction, while $f$ is the normal velocity width, with normal position width $\ell f$ after a polynomial shear. The models therefore use different test weights: $r^4f^{1-\eta}$ in the round model and $r^{3+\eta}f^{1-\eta}$ in the cylinder, where $0<\eta<1$. These windows and their weights are defined in Definitions <a href="#cyl:def-test" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cyl:def-test">15</a> and <a href="#rt:regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rt:regularity">91</a>.

Suppose the initial packet measure has total energy $e$ and obeys $\mu(Q)\le\kappa w(Q)$ for every test. At the final cut, let $m_\lambda$ be the energy assigned to a test of weight $w_\lambda$. The index $\lambda$ includes both its time interval and its test; assignments may be fractional, but their sum at each interval is bounded by that interval’s row energy. The normalized cubic sum is <a id="eq:intro-functional"></a>$$\label{eq:intro-functional}
 \mathcal B_s=
 \frac{s^{-1/2}}{e\sqrt\kappa}
 \sum_\lambda\frac{m_\lambda^{3/2}}{\sqrt{w_\lambda}}.$$ Here $s$ is the ratio between final and initial time lengths, and the sum includes all final intervals. In the physical application $s=H$ and the terminal tests have weights comparable to one, recovering the mass sum above. Theorem <a href="#thm:round" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:round">104</a> bounds $\mathcal B_s$ with a scale loss that tends to zero with $\eta$ and the subsequent losses. Section <a href="#sec:phys" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:phys">10</a> verifies the required initial regularity on the physical time slice and completes the frequency summation.

The model bounds are proved by contradiction. Suppose that the cubic sum has a growth exponent larger than the permitted $\eta$-dependent loss. In the cylinder model, an extremal reduction selects homogeneous mass and weight data. Any ordinary regularity split that preserves the extremal exponent must attain the corresponding energy and regularity bounds at the level of exponents. Comparing the retained tests then controls both their polynomial shears and their widths at successive cuts. After a further reduction, the width exponents are affine functions of depth. The lower-dimensional wave and incidence estimates exclude the configurations in which both normalized shear costs vanish.

For the remaining configurations, we study a finite phase name at time depth $a$ and horizontal resolution $v$. It records bins for time, direction, base position, and the normal phase after subtracting a recorded shear. From its normalized entropy we subtract the baseline prescribed by regularity, the test weight, and the extremal mass data. The resulting entropy excess is nonnegative. At specified boundary resolutions, recovery of the name from a retained test label gives the matching upper bound, so the excess vanishes there. Conditional sampling supplies auxiliary probes, but the quantity ultimately estimated remains the entropy of this one phase name. Planar incidence and local projection estimates give directions in which the excess must decrease when followed backwards from those boundary points. Constructing a path that stays in the domain of the applicable inequalities gives the contradiction to nonnegativity. The admissible directions depend on the shear profile; unit-cost boundaries and intervals with no angular entropy growth require separate estimates.

To pass from the cylinder to the round velocity surface $(A,|A|^2)$, $A\in\mathbb R^2$, we transfer thin round tests to cylindrical ones. If one coordinate remains quantum, this transfer retains its one-dimensional Schrödinger evolution. The remaining round configurations are excluded by a separate entropy argument, first for classical rays and then for waves. Finally, input regularity is verified on the original physical time slice before summing the dyadic frequency estimates.

The paper is organized as follows. Definitions <a href="#cyl:def-states" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cyl:def-states">14</a>, <a href="#cyl:def-test" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cyl:def-test">15</a>, and <a href="#cyl:def-setup" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cyl:def-setup">16</a> specify the cylinder states, tests, and fixed setups; Proposition <a href="#cyl:affine" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cyl:affine">29</a> gives the extremal configurations used in the subsequent argument. Section <a href="#sec:low" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:low">4</a> supplies the lower-dimensional estimates. Definition <a href="#names:canonical-name" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="names:canonical-name">49</a> introduces the canonical names, and Proposition <a href="#names:canonical-entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="names:canonical-entropy">51</a> defines their entropy excess. Section <a href="#int:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="int:section">6</a> derives the local inequalities, which Section <a href="#act:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="act:section">7</a> uses in the proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:cylinder" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cylinder">19</a>. Definitions <a href="#rt:model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rt:model">90</a> and <a href="#rt:regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rt:regularity">91</a> specify the round experiment and its tests. Proposition <a href="#rt:thin-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rt:thin-exclusion">97</a> is the thin-shape reduction used in Theorem <a href="#thm:round" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:round">104</a>; Section <a href="#sec:phys" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:phys">10</a> then makes the passage to the physical wave. Section <a href="#sec:bochner-riesz" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:bochner-riesz">11</a> derives the maximal and nonmaximal Fourier-summation consequences and records their standard restriction and Kakeya implications.

<div class="samepage">

The principal technical steps are the extremal reduction with compatible shears, the phase-name calculus, and the uniform transfer of wave packets on thin gaps. These intermediate results are formulated for the packet models considered here, independently of the final frequency summation. Throughout, finite operator stacks and polynomial cutoff bounds are fixed before taking a scale limit; Section <a href="#sec:framework" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:framework">2</a> specifies the order of all subsequent limits.

</div>

<a id="sec:framework"></a>
### Scales, energies, and limiting arguments

The arguments below compare experiments whose parameters and probability spaces vary with scale. This section records the meaning of those comparisons. It does not assert that a geometrically defined subexperiment is admissible: its support, regularity, and operator bounds must be checked in the section where it is constructed.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
#### Fixed setups and exponent bounds

We use dyadic scales $s=2^{-n}$ tending to zero. A depth $a$ represents the scale $s^a$. Replacing it by the nearest dyadic scale changes a positive quantity by a bounded factor and hence changes its normalized logarithm by $O(1/\log(1/s))$. Width exponents and growth exponents have opposite sign conventions: $$\operatorname{width\ exponent}(r)=\frac{\log r}{\log s},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{growth\ exponent}(B)=\frac{\log B}{\log(1/s)}.$$ The growth exponent of a zero quantity is $-\infty$.

<a id="stmt-def-fw-setup"></a>
<div id="def:fw-setup" class="definition">

**Definition 2** (Fixed polynomial setup). A fixed polynomial setup specifies all structural constants, the finite upper bounds on powers of $s^{-1}$ occurring in its hypotheses, and a finite bound on the number of operations along each branch. These data are fixed before $s\to0$. A sequence in this setup may have parameters, operators, measures, and Hilbert spaces depending on $s$, provided the specified bounds hold uniformly along the sequence.

An error $r_s$ is negligible relative to a positive reference quantity $a_s$ if, for every $N>0$, $$|r_s|\le C_N s^N a_s$$ for all sufficiently small scales, with $C_N$ independent of scale. For a family of choices at each scale, uniform negligibility means that the same constants and scale thresholds work for every choice. The reference quantity is always specified; it may be an input energy or an operator norm. Polynomially many errors can be added without losing negligibility when their reference quantities and polynomial bounds are controlled uniformly.

</div>

<a id="eq:fw-upper-exponent"></a>
For a nonnegative functional $\mathcal B_s$, define its upper exponent to be $$\label{eq:fw-upper-exponent}
 \Gamma=\sup_{\mathscr S}\ \sup_{(s_k,\mathcal E_k)}
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \frac{\log\mathcal B_{s_k}(\mathcal E_k)}{\log(1/s_k)}.$$ Here $\mathscr S$ ranges over fixed polynomial setups, and the inner supremum ranges over admissible sequences in that setup with $s_k\to0$. The particular model specifies which setups are allowed. The finiteness of $\Gamma$ must be proved for that model.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-uniform"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-uniform" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:fw-uniform-bound"></a>
**Lemma 3** (Uniform bound within a fixed setup). *Suppose $\Gamma\in\mathbb R$ in <a href="#eq:fw-upper-exponent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-upper-exponent">[eq:fw-upper-exponent]</a>. Fix a family $\mathcal A_s$ such that every sequence of choices $\mathcal E_k\in\mathcal A_{s_k}$, $s_k\to0$, is admissible in one fixed polynomial setup. In particular, all negligible tail hypotheses are uniform over this family. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $s_0>0$ such that $$\label{eq:fw-uniform-bound}
 \mathcal B_s(\mathcal E)\le s^{-\Gamma-\varepsilon}
 \qquad(0<s<s_0,\ \mathcal E\in\mathcal A_s).$$ If the functional is also uniformly bounded on this family at each of the finitely many larger dyadic scales under consideration, then <a href="#eq:fw-uniform-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-uniform-bound">[eq:fw-uniform-bound]</a> holds on the entire scale range after inserting a constant $C_{\varepsilon,\mathscr S}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-uniform"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-uniform</summary>

*Proof.* Failure of the first assertion provides $s_k\to0$ and $\mathcal E_k\in\mathcal A_{s_k}$ with $\mathcal B_{s_k}(\mathcal E_k)>s_k^{-\Gamma-\varepsilon}$. The resulting sequence is admissible in the fixed setup and has upper exponent at least $\Gamma+\varepsilon$, contradicting <a href="#eq:fw-upper-exponent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-upper-exponent">[eq:fw-upper-exponent]</a>. For the second assertion, take the maximum of the finitely many required constants at the remaining scales and $1$. ◻

</details>

The constant in Lemma <a href="#lem:fw-uniform" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:fw-uniform">3</a> may depend on every bound fixed in Definition <a href="#def:fw-setup" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:fw-setup">2</a>. It is not uniform when those bounds grow along an outer approximation. Conversely, a failure of an estimate with a fixed positive exponent slack can be disproved within one fixed setup, even when that setup was selected late in an outer argument.

<a id="stmt-rem-fw-small-pieces"></a>
<div id="rem:fw-small-pieces" class="remark">

*Remark 4* (Small normalized pieces). Changing the reference energy can change a tail hypothesis. For example, an error negligible relative to $e$ is negligible relative to $e'$ whenever $e'/e\ge s^C$ for some fixed $C$, but this implication does not hold for arbitrary $e'>0$. Applications to a collection of subexperiments must therefore either verify the hypotheses relative to each new energy, or use a direct estimate on pieces with superpolynomially small energy. No uniformity assertion in Lemma <a href="#lem:fw-uniform" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:fw-uniform">3</a> supplies this missing verification.

</div>

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
#### Energy and finite extraction

Energy means a squared Hilbert norm. Input energy at a time interval means the energy before the evolutions and masks being estimated. When a time interval is subdivided, its input is copied into its descendants. Consequently the sum of input energies over distinct starting intervals need not be bounded by the original energy. This sum will always be distinguished from the energy available to one interval.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-energy"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-energy" class="lemma">

**Lemma 5** (Disjoint row restrictions and copies). *Let $V:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry and let $P_1,\ldots,P_N$ be mutually orthogonal projections on $\mathcal K$. For $g_j=V^*P_jVg$, <a id="eq:fw-row-energy"></a>$$\label{eq:fw-row-energy}
 \sum_{j=1}^N\lVert g_j\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2
 \le\sum_{j=1}^N\lVert P_jVg\rVert_{\mathcal K}^2
 \le\lVert g\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2.$$ If $\sum_jP_jVg=Vg$, then $\sum_jg_j=g$. By contrast, for $N$ contractions $T_j$ applied to separate copies of $g$, the general bound is only $\sum_j\lVert T_jg\rVert^2\le N\lVert g\rVert^2$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-energy"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-energy</summary>

*Proof.* The adjoint $V^*$ has norm one. Apply this fact to each $P_jVg$ and then use orthogonality. The reconstruction assertion follows from $V^*V=\mathrm{Id}$. The assertion about copies follows by applying $\lVert T_jg\rVert\le\lVert g\rVert$ separately to each $j$. ◻

</details>

The projections in Lemma <a href="#lem:fw-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:fw-energy">5</a> may be multiplication by disjoint measurable row sets in a direct integral. Their synthesized images need not be orthogonal. For the weighted sums used here, this is accommodated by a norm inequality, not by an orthogonality claim.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-finite-extraction"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-finite-extraction" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (Extraction from finitely many classes). *Let $q\ge1$, and suppose that a nonnegative functional $F$ satisfies $$F(g_1+\cdots+g_N)^{1/q}
 \le\sum_{j=1}^N F(g_j)^{1/q}.$$ Then some $j$ satisfies $F(g_j)\ge N^{-q}F(\sum_i g_i)$. Consequently, if $N=N_s$ obeys $\log N_s/\log(1/s)\to0$, passing to a maximizing class costs zero growth exponent. The same conclusion holds for a fixed finite number of successive such extractions. To use the conclusion for a model exponent, each selected class must itself be admissible in a fixed setup.*

<a id="eq:fw-cube-seminorm"></a>
*In particular, for linear maps $A_\lambda$ into Hilbert spaces and positive weights $w_\lambda$, $$\label{eq:fw-cube-seminorm}
 F(g)=\sum_\lambda w_\lambda^{-1/2}\lVert A_\lambda g\rVert^3$$ has the required inequality with $q=3$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-finite-extraction"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-finite-extraction</summary>

*Proof.* The right side of the assumed inequality is at most $N\max_jF(g_j)^{1/q}$. Raising to the $q$th power proves the extraction estimate. Its logarithmic loss is $q\log N_s/\log(1/s)$; finitely many such losses still tend to zero. For <a href="#eq:fw-cube-seminorm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-cube-seminorm">[eq:fw-cube-seminorm]</a>, $F(g)^{1/3}$ is the norm of $(w_\lambda^{-1/6}A_\lambda g)_\lambda$ in the corresponding $\ell^3$ sum of Hilbert spaces, and Minkowski’s inequality applies. For a countable label set, apply the inequality first to finite subsets and then use monotone convergence. ◻

</details>

A separate elementary extraction will be used when energies are already summable: if $0<E<\infty$, $A>0$, $a_j\ge0$, $e_j\ge0$, $\sum_j e_j\le E$, and $\sum_j a_j\ge A$, then $\sup_{j:e_j>0}a_j/e_j\ge A/E$, provided $a_j=0$ whenever $e_j=0$. Indeed the contrary strict upper bound, multiplied by $e_j$ and summed, contradicts the two hypotheses. Any additional count or regularity constraints on the chosen class require their own discard estimates.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
#### Closure of exponent data

For a finite list of positive quantities, exponent data are the limits of their normalized logarithms along admissible sequences, when these limits exist and are finite. We may also take the closure of such data in a fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space. This outer closure permits a different fixed polynomial setup for each approximating sequence. It does not turn these sequences into one admissible sequence with unbounded setup parameters.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-closure"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-closure" class="lemma">

**Lemma 7** (Extrema of bounded exponent data). *Let $K\subset\mathbb R^{m+1}$ be a nonempty compact set of feasible limiting data $(g,x_1,\ldots,x_m)$. Set $G=\max_K g$, minimize $x_1$ on $K\cap\{g=G\}$, and then successively minimize $x_j$ on the slice where all preceding extrema are attained. Every slice is nonempty and compact, and every stated minimum is attained.*

*The attainment assertions, and nonemptiness and closedness of the successive slices, remain valid for a possibly noncompact closed set $K$ under the following hypotheses: $g$ has a finite supremum and a bounded maximizing sequence in $K$, and each successive coordinate has a finite infimum and a bounded minimizing sequence within the preceding extremal slice. This alternative does not assert compactness of the slices. A new coordinate may be added to the tuple only after the required boundedness and feasibility have been proved for the enlarged tuple.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-closure"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-closure</summary>

*Proof.* A continuous coordinate function attains its extremum on a nonempty compact set. The set where that extremum is attained is closed in the same compact set and is nonempty. Induction proves the first assertion. For the alternative, pass first to a convergent subsequence of the bounded maximizing sequence. Closedness and continuity attain the supremum of $g$. At each subsequent step, pass to a convergent subsequence of the stipulated bounded minimizing sequence. Closedness preserves feasibility, and continuity of the coordinates preserves the preceding equalities and attains the next infimum. Each resulting slice is a nonempty intersection of closed sets. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rem-fw-extra-coordinate"></a>
<div id="rem:fw-extra-coordinate" class="remark">

*Remark 8*. Boundedness of a new coordinate cannot be inferred from compactness of previously chosen coordinates. For example, the closure of the projection of $\{(p,c):c\ge1,\ p=1/c\}$ onto the $p$ axis contains $p=0$, although the closure of the full set has no finite point with $p=0$. Thus a geometric bound on the curvature cost at the already chosen growth and mass exponents is an essential part of a curvature minimization argument.

</div>

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-strict-improvement"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-strict-improvement" class="lemma">

**Lemma 9** (Strict improvement in a closure). *Let $K\subset\mathbb R^{k+1}$ be a closed set of feasible data. Suppose that $c_0$ is the minimum of the last coordinate $c$ on the nonempty slice $K\cap\{z=z_0\}$. There cannot be data $(z_n,c_n)\in K$ with $z_n\to z_0$ and $\limsup_n c_n<c_0$, provided $(c_n)$ is bounded below and has a bounded subsequence. In particular, a construction contradicts minimality when its preceding exponents converge to the specified extrema and its cost improves by a fixed positive amount in the units of the constructed experiment.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-strict-improvement"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-strict-improvement</summary>

*Proof.* Pass to a convergent subsequence of $(c_n)$. Its limit $c$ is strictly less than $c_0$. Closedness places $(z_0,c)$ in the minimizing slice, which is a contradiction. ◻

</details>

These lemmas assert neither an exactly extremizing input nor an infinite chain of operators. A construction at limiting exponent data must be performed on approximating finite experiments. The estimates must then imply the asserted bounds on a convergent subsequence of the finite tuples actually used.

<a id="pm-h-9"></a>
#### Ordered limits and changes of scale

At a depth gap $h>0$, the new basic scale is $\delta=s^h$. A factor $s^{-\alpha}$ has growth exponent $\alpha/h$ in these new units. Consequently a loss tending to zero in the original units is harmless on a fixed gap, but it is harmless on shrinking gaps only after it has been made $o(h)$.

All uses of mesh refinement or tangent gaps have the following order. First fix the positive gap, the finite list of cuts and observations, and all cutoff depths needed for that comparison. In each fixed polynomial setup take the scale limit. Next make the preceding approximation errors and mesh errors as small as required relative to that fixed gap. Only then shrink the gap or enlarge the finite list. When further tangent layers are used, their positive lengths and required accuracies are fixed before the preceding tangent limit is taken. Each application of a model exponent is to an admissible sequence at a fixed stage of these outer choices.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-pullback"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-pullback" class="lemma">

**Lemma 10** (Pullback of a strict exponent contradiction). *Let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R$ be an upper exponent as in <a href="#eq:fw-upper-exponent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-upper-exponent">[eq:fw-upper-exponent]</a>. Suppose that, for each integer $m$, a construction produces an admissible sequence in a fixed setup $\mathscr S_m$ with upper exponent at least $\Gamma+\tau-r_m$, where $\tau>0$ is fixed and $r_m\to0$. Then such a construction is impossible. The setup need not be uniform in $m$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-pullback"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-pullback</summary>

*Proof.* Choose one fixed $m$ with $r_m<\tau/2$. The sequence in $\mathscr S_m$ then contradicts the definition of $\Gamma$. ◻

</details>

Having one favorable scale for each $m$ would not satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma <a href="#lem:fw-pullback" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:fw-pullback">10</a>. For example, the quantities $B_m(2^{-n})$, equal to $2^n$ when $n=m$ and equal to $1$ otherwise, have upper exponent zero for every fixed $m$ but exponent one along the diagonal $m=n$. We will therefore use a diagonal of scales for probability comparisons only after the necessary model estimates with strict slack have been established in their fixed setups.

<a id="pm-h-10"></a>
#### Elementary probability comparisons

All random variables below are evaluated under the probability law specified at that point of the argument. A conditional probability may condition on a continuous variable or a sigma-algebra. We use natural logarithms. Under a law $P$, for a finite-valued name $X$, write $$H_P(X\mid Y)=-\mathbb E_P\log P(X\mid Y).$$ Relative entropy is $\operatorname{KL}(P\Vert Q)=\int\log(dP/dQ)\,dP$ when $P\ll Q$, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. Conditional mutual information is $$I_P(X;V\mid Y)
 =\mathbb E_{P_Y}\operatorname{KL}
   \bigl(P_{X,V\mid Y}\Vert P_{X\mid Y}\otimes P_{V\mid Y}\bigr).$$ This definition also permits continuous variables; when $X$ is finite, it equals $H_P(X\mid Y)-H_P(X\mid V,Y)$. For $0<\rho<1$, the scale-normalized quantities are $H_\rho=H_P/\log(1/\rho)$ and $I_\rho=I_P/\log(1/\rho)$, with the law indicated when it changes. For a finite-valued name $X$ and conditioning data $Y$, write <a id="eq:fw-score"></a>$$\label{eq:fw-score}
 i_s(X\mid Y)
   =-\frac{\log\mathbb P(X\mid Y)}{\log(1/s)},$$ where the conditional probability is evaluated at the sampled value of $X$. Values on null events are immaterial. Thus $H_s(X\mid Y)=\mathbb E_P i_s(X\mid Y)$: the score is random, whereas entropy and mutual information are averaged quantities.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-capacity"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-capacity" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:fw-capacity"></a>
**Lemma 11** (Capacity tails). *Suppose that, given $Y$, the variable $X$ has at most $N$ possible values almost surely. For every $u\ge0$, $$\label{eq:fw-capacity}
 \mathbb P\bigl\{\mathbb P(X\mid Y)<e^{-u}/N\bigr\}\le e^{-u}.$$ If $N\le s^{-C}$ for a fixed $C$, then $\mathbb P\{i_s(X\mid Y)>C+t\}\le s^t$ for $t\ge0$. These normalized scores are uniformly integrable as $s\to0$. In particular, convergence in probability to a finite constant implies convergence of their expectations to that constant.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-capacity"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-capacity</summary>

*Proof.* For each conditioning value, sum the conditional probabilities of the at most $N$ values below $e^{-u}/N$, and then integrate. This proves <a href="#eq:fw-capacity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-capacity">[eq:fw-capacity]</a> and its normalized version. For $K>C$, the tail integral identity gives $$\mathbb E\bigl[i_s(X\mid Y)\mathbf 1_{\{i_s(X\mid Y)>K\}}\bigr]
 \le s^{K-C}\left(K+\frac1{\log(1/s)}\right).$$ For $s\le1/2$ the right side tends to zero uniformly as $K\to\infty$. This is uniform integrability; truncation at $K$ proves the final assertion. ◻

</details>

The same estimate applies to a relative name with at most $N$ refinements after its parent has been included in the conditioning. It does not require a bounded number of values for the conditioning data. When absolute names have unbounded capacity exponents along an outer limit, the lemma supplies uniform integrability only for the relative names whose capacities have been bounded.

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-restriction"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-restriction" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:fw-restriction"></a>
**Lemma 12** (Stability under restriction). *Let $Q=P(\,\cdot\mid E)$, where $P(E)=q>0$, and let $X$ be a finite name with arbitrary conditioning data $Y$. If $q\ge s^\alpha$, then, outside a set of $Q$-probability at most $2s^\tau$, $$\label{eq:fw-restriction}
 \lvert i_s^Q(X\mid Y)-i_s^P(X\mid Y)\rvert\le\alpha+\tau
 \qquad(\tau>0).$$ Consequently, restrictions with $q=s^{o(1)}$ preserve deterministic limiting scores, provided their previous exceptional probabilities are negligible relative to $q$. On a gap with scale $s^h$, the corresponding condition is $\log(1/q)=o(h\log(1/s))$ and all errors are divided by $h$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-restriction"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-restriction</summary>

*Proof.* For the marginal of any variable $W$, the likelihood ratio $L_W=dQ_W/dP_W$ is $P(E\mid W)/q$, hence is at most $1/q$. Moreover $Q\{L_W<s^\tau\}\le s^\tau$ by integrating $L_W$ against $P_W$. Apply these two facts to $W=(X,Y)$ and $W=Y$. Except on the union of the two exceptional sets, both ratios belong to $[s^\tau,s^{-\alpha}]$. The conditional likelihood ratio is $L_{(X,Y)}/L_Y$, so it belongs to $[s^{\alpha+\tau},s^{-\alpha-\tau}]$. Taking logarithms proves <a href="#eq:fw-restriction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-restriction">[eq:fw-restriction]</a>. An old exceptional event of $P$-probability $r$ has $Q$-probability at most $r/q$, proving the stated qualification and the consequences. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-fw-information"></a>
<div id="lem:fw-information" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:fw-information-restriction"></a>
**Lemma 13** (Negligible information and positive restrictions). *Let $U,V$ be finite names, with arbitrary conditioning data $Y$. Put $L=\log(1/s)$ and $$j=\log\frac{P(U\mid V,Y)}{P(U\mid Y)}.$$ Then $P\{j<-r\}\le e^{-r}$ for $r\ge0$, and $\mathbb Ej=I_P(U;V\mid Y)$. If $I_P(U;V\mid Y)=o(L)$, then $j/L\to0$ in probability. If $Q=P(\,\cdot\mid E)$ and $P(E)\ge q_0>0$, then $$\label{eq:fw-information-restriction}
 I_Q(U;V\mid Y)
 \le\frac{I_P(U;V\mid Y)+\log2}{q_0}.$$ In particular such restrictions preserve $o(L)$ information budgets. No such conclusion is asserted for arbitrary events of probability $s^{o(1)}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-fw-information"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-fw-information</summary>

*Proof.* Condition on $Y$ and compare the joint law of $(U,V)$ with the product of its conditional marginals. At actual samples their likelihood ratio is $e^j$, so integrating over the set where it is less than $e^{-r}$ proves the tail bound. Therefore $\mathbb E(j_-)\le1$, while the definition of conditional mutual information gives $\mathbb Ej=I_P(U;V\mid Y)$. It follows that $\mathbb E(j_+)\le I_P(U;V\mid Y)+1$. Markov’s inequality and the negative tail bound prove convergence in probability after division by $L$.

Let $B=\mathbf 1_E$. The chain rule gives $$I_P(U;V\mid Y,B)
 \le I_P(U;V,B\mid Y)
 \le I_P(U;V\mid Y)+H_P(B\mid V,Y)
 \le I_P(U;V\mid Y)+\log2.$$ The left side is the average, over the two values of $B$, of the corresponding conditional mutual informations. Its contribution from $B=1$ is $P(E)I_Q(U;V\mid Y)$, proving <a href="#eq:fw-information-restriction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:fw-information-restriction">[eq:fw-information-restriction]</a>. ◻

</details>

The elementary comparisons in this subsection refer to actual laws and finite lists of names. Later score limits may be obtained from joint weak subsequences of those finite lists; no convergence of conditional sampling kernels is required or asserted. Extending the limits to a dense set of depth queries requires the specific nesting and list bounds proved for those names. In particular, these probability lemmas neither couple input and output packet marginals through a quantum mask nor transfer a profile between different measuring laws without a separate argument.

<a id="sec:cylinder"></a>
### Cylinder experiments and extremal configurations

This section defines the two cylinder models and constructs the configurations used in the cylinder estimates. A state is measured by its squared Hilbert norm. Time subdivision copies that state into its descendant intervals; it does not divide its energy among them. This distinction explains the growth factor in the normalization below.

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### States, tests, and assignments

Fix $0<\eta<1$ and $s=2^{-n}$. A cut of length $\ell=2^{-k}$, with $0\le k\le n$, consists of the dyadic subintervals of $[0,1)$ of that length. The final cut has length $s$ and contains exactly $s^{-1}$ intervals. We measure an interval at its left endpoint $T$. There are finitely many operator cuts, in nonincreasing order of length; repeated cuts are permitted. Their number is bounded on each polynomial setup. Every child receives the freely evolved state of its parent, with the operators specified on that branch.

<a id="cyl:base-flow"></a>
The exact base index is $F=(X,B,Y)$, with $$\label{cyl:base-flow}
 B_T=B+TX,\qquad Y_T=Y+TX^2.$$ Additional exact indices range over standard Borel spaces; arbitrary separable Hilbert multiplicities are allowed. All integrals and squared norms include these indices. One may equivalently use a measurable direct integral of separable Hilbert spaces over such an index space.

<a id="stmt-cyl-def-states"></a>
<div id="cyl:def-states" class="definition">

**Definition 14** (Cylinder states). In the *classical cylinder*, $(N,D)$ is another exact index, $D_T=D+TN$, and free evolution leaves the state unchanged in these moving coordinates. In the *hybrid cylinder*, $H>0$ is fixed, there is an exact index $\sigma\in[1,2]$, and a fiber state belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R_D;\mathcal H)$. Its free propagator $U_t^{H,\sigma}$ is $$\widehat{U_t^{H,\sigma}g}(p)
       =e^{-itHp^2/(2\sigma)}\widehat g(p).$$ At length $\ell$, set $$d_\ell=(H/\ell)^{1/2},\qquad q_\ell=(H\ell)^{1/2},
 \qquad
 \phi_{D,N}^{\ell,\sigma}(z)
  =(\pi q_\ell^2)^{-1/4}
    e^{-(z-D)^2/(2q_\ell^2)+i\sigma Nz/H}.$$ The analysis operator is $$(V_\ell g)(D,N)=\langle g,\phi_{D,N}^{\ell,\sigma}\rangle,
 \qquad d\nu_\sigma(D,N)=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi H}\,dD\,dN.$$ For the classical model, $V_\ell=\mathrm{Id}$ and $d_\ell=0$. An admissible operator at a cut is $V_\ell^*MV_\ell$, where $M$ is a measurable pointwise contraction on the multiplicity space and preserves all exact indices. The row measure $\mu_I$ is the squared norm of the analyzed state, possibly restricted by row assignments.

</div>

With the Fourier normalization of Section <a href="#sec:introduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:introduction">1</a>, Plancherel in $N$ gives $$\int_\mathbb R\lvert \langle g,\phi_{D,N}^{\ell,\sigma}\rangle\rvert^2
                   \frac{\sigma\,dN}{2\pi H}
 =\int_\mathbb R\lVert g(z)\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2
             (\pi q_\ell^2)^{-1/2}e^{-(z-D)^2/q_\ell^2}\,dz.$$ Integration in $D$ proves $V_\ell^*V_\ell=\mathrm{Id}$. In particular, every admissible operator is a contraction. The packet parameter $D$ in the hybrid model is an observation coordinate, not an exact classical index.

<a id="stmt-cyl-def-test"></a>
<div id="cyl:def-test" class="definition">

<a id="cyl:velocity-test"></a>
<a id="cyl:position-test"></a>
**Definition 15** (Cylinder tests). A test $Q$ at $(T,\ell)$ has widths $r>0$, $f\ge d_\ell$, with $f>0$. For a hybrid row observed at the cut $T$, $D_T$ in the following inequalities denotes its instantaneous analyzed center $D$, not an exact classical trajectory. The test is specified by <a id="cyl:base-test"></a>$$\begin{gathered}
 |X-x|\le r,\qquad |B_T-b|\le\ell r,\qquad
 |Y_T-y-2x(B_T-b)|\le\ell r^2,\label{cyl:base-test}\\
 |N-c-\alpha X-\beta(T)X^2-K(Y_T-2XB_T)|\le f,
 \label{cyl:velocity-test}\\
 |D_T-d-\alpha B_T-\beta(T)Y_T+KB_T^2|\le\ell f.
 \label{cyl:position-test}
\end{gathered}$$ All centers and coefficients are real. Extend the coefficients by $$\beta(t)=\beta(T)+(t-T)K,\qquad d(t)=d+(t-T)c.$$ The test weight is $w(Q)=r^{3+\eta}f^{1-\eta}$. A row measure is $\kappa$-regular if $\mu(Q)\le\kappa w(Q)$ for every admissible test.

</div>

If the expressions subtracted from $N,D_T$ in Equations <a href="#cyl:velocity-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:velocity-test">[cyl:velocity-test]</a>–<a href="#cyl:position-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:position-test">[cyl:position-test]</a> are $A(F)$ and $S_t(F)$, respectively, direct differentiation gives $\partial_t A=0$ and $\partial_t S_t=A$. Also <a id="cyl:derivative"></a>$$\label{cyl:derivative}
 P(F)=\alpha+2\beta(t)X-2KB_t$$ is independent of $t$.

<a id="cyl:functional"></a>
An assignment to the final cut is a family of nonnegative row measures $\mu_\lambda\le\mu_I$, each supported on a test $Q_\lambda$ at its own interval, such that $\sum_{\lambda\text{ at }I}\mu_\lambda\le\mu_I$. Fractional assignments are allowed. Put $m_\lambda=\mu_\lambda(Q_\lambda)$ and $w_\lambda=w(Q_\lambda)$. If $e>0$ is the root energy and the root row measure is $\kappa$-regular, define $$\label{cyl:functional}
 \mathcal B_s
  =\frac{s^{-1/2}}{e\sqrt\kappa}
           \sum_\lambda\frac{m_\lambda^{3/2}}{\sqrt{w_\lambda}}.$$ The sum includes all final intervals. Bounded enlargements of the defining inequalities are interchangeable with a bounded change of the weight: enlarge $r,f$ by fixed constants or cover by finitely many translates.

<a id="pm-h-13"></a>
#### Cutoffs and localization

<a id="stmt-cyl-def-setup"></a>
<div id="cyl:def-setup" class="definition">

**Definition 16** (Polynomial cylinder setup). The quantities $e/\kappa,\kappa/e$ and, in the hybrid case, $H,H^{-1}$ are bounded by fixed powers of $s^{-1}$. The initial base support lies in a box of fixed-power size. The initial normal phase has negligible mass relative to $e$ outside such a box. The marginal base density and the joint density in $(X,B,Y,N,D)$ are bounded by $e$ times a fixed power of $s^{-1}$, with respect to Lebesgue measure. Negligibility is uniform within each family to which an exponent bound is applied. All these powers, and the bound on the number of operators on a branch, are fixed before $s\to0$.

</div>

The exponent closure may use successively larger fixed powers, in the ordered sense specified in the framework. It never replaces the inner scale limit by isolated scales with increasing cutoff powers.

<a id="stmt-cyl-localization"></a>
<div id="cyl:localization" class="lemma">

**Lemma 17** (Symmetries and Gaussian localization). *The models are invariant under translations, base boosts, dilation in base units $(r,r,r^2)$, normal dilation, affine time normalization, and subtraction of one common normal shear of Equations <a href="#cyl:velocity-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:velocity-test">[cyl:velocity-test]</a>–<a href="#cyl:position-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:position-test">[cyl:position-test]</a>. All operators and assignments must be transformed with the state.*

<a id="cyl:correspondence"></a>
*For $\ell'\le\ell$, $|t|\le C\ell$, and fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the hybrid frame transfer is negligible in operator norm outside $$\label{cyl:correspondence}
 |N'-N|\le s^{-\varepsilon}d_{\ell'},\qquad
 |D'-D-tN|\le s^{-\varepsilon}q_\ell.$$ This remains true along any fixed finite stack of masks and after summing over a polynomial number of intervals. At a repeated cut, synthesis and reanalysis of a restricted $\kappa$-regular row measure produce a $C_\eta\kappa$-regular measure. The same assertion holds for truncated families of tests whenever the normal enlargements in the proof belong to that family or are covered by translates belonging to it.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cyl-localization"><summary>Proof of stmt-cyl-localization</summary>

*Proof.* A base boost replaces $X$ by $X-x_0$ and replaces the last base position by its appropriate linear tilt in $B_t$; Equation <a href="#cyl:base-flow" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:base-flow">[cyl:base-flow]</a> then has the same form. A common normal shear subtracts $a(F)$ from velocity and $b(F)+ta(F)$ from position. On each hybrid fiber it is a Weyl translation, and the free propagator intertwines the two translations up to a scalar phase. The scalar phase can be included in the conjugated mask. If a time interval of length $L$ is normalized to unit length, positions are divided by $L$, velocities are unchanged, and $H$ becomes $H/L$. Dividing normal coordinates and velocities by $F_0$ changes $H$ to $H/F_0^2$. Dividing base coordinates by $(r_0,r_0,r_0^2)$ and normal coordinates by $F_0$ divides all weights by $A=r_0^{3+\eta}F_0^{1-\eta}$ and multiplies the regularity constant by $A$. Energy is preserved by the corresponding unitary coordinate changes. Thus Equation <a href="#cyl:functional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cyl:functional">[cyl:functional]</a> is unchanged.

The scalar transfer kernel is $\langle U_t^{H,\sigma}\phi_{D,N}^{\ell,\sigma},\phi_{D',N'}^{\ell',\sigma}\rangle$. Free propagation changes the first packet’s position width to at most $Cq_\ell$, since $|t|H/q_\ell\le Cq_\ell$, and leaves its Fourier width comparable to $q_\ell^{-1}$. Integrating two Gaussians, in physical space for the position difference and in Fourier space for the momentum difference, gives an upper bound of the form $$C_s\exp\left[-c\left(
       \frac{|D'-D-tN|^2}{q_\ell^2}
       +\frac{|N'-N|^2}{d_{\ell'}^2}\right)\right],$$ where $C_s$ and the Schur integration volumes have only fixed-power costs on the setup. Each of the two separate Gaussian bounds implies the displayed joint bound after reducing $c$. Schur’s test therefore makes the discarded kernel smaller than every power of $s$. A finite product and a polynomial sum preserve this conclusion. If no chain of the correspondences connects two row sets, the operator between those sets is negligible; this statement does not require a positive-kernel description of its main part.

At a repeated cut the absolute kernel is exactly $$\exp\left(-\frac{(D-D')^2}{4q_\ell^2}
           -\frac{\sigma^2(N-N')^2}{4d_\ell^2}\right).$$ Its Schur norms are bounded independently of $H,\ell$. Cauchy–Schwarz against this kernel bounds output energy on a test by a Gaussian-weighted sum of input energies on its normal enlargements. Since $f\ge d_\ell$ and $\ell f\ge q_\ell$, the enlargement in the $j$th Gaussian shell is obtained by multiplying the normal width by $C(1+j)$.
