 \label{eq:phys-frequency-change}$$ Thus the same function, denoted by $v$, is exactly $$v(t,b,y)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int
 e^{i(b\cdot\eta-y\rho-t|\eta|^2/(4\rho))}
 J(\eta,\rho)a_H(\xi(\eta,\rho))
 \widehat g(\xi(\eta,\rho))\,d\eta\,d\rho.
 \label{eq:phys-round-state}$$ It is therefore a free round-cone wave. Its energy is independent of $t$ and satisfies $$e:=\lVert v(t)\rVert_2^2
 =(2\pi)^{-3}\int J(\eta(\xi),\rho(\xi))
          |a_H(\xi)\widehat g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi
 \le C\lVert g\rVert_2^2.
 \label{eq:phys-energy}$$ In particular the map from $g$ to any plateau-analyzed state $V_1v(T)$ has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm. This assertion remains true after replacing $g$ by its restriction to any measurable subset of $K$.

<a id="eq:phys-small-energy"></a>
<a id="eq:phys-energy-range"></a>
The bounded physical output region is covered by finitely many unit intervals $[T,T+1]$ in $t$, with bounded $T$. We work on one such interval. Write $B=\lVert g\rVert_\infty$, and suppose first that $g\in L^\infty$ is supported in $K$. If $B=0$ or $e=0$, the asserted estimate is immediate. The frequency support in $(\eta,-\rho)$ has volume $O(H^{-3})$, so Cauchy–Schwarz in Fourier space gives <a id="eq:phys-bernstein"></a>$$\lVert v(t)\rVert_\infty\le C H^{-3/2}\sqrt e.
 \label{eq:phys-bernstein}$$ If $e<H^{10}B^2$, then $$\int_T^{T+1}\int |v|^3
 \le C H^{-3/2}e^{3/2}
 \le C B\lVert g\rVert_2^2.
 \label{eq:phys-small-energy}$$ We may therefore assume $$H^{10}B^2\le e\le C\lVert g\rVert_2^2\le C_K B^2.
 \label{eq:phys-energy-range}$$

<a id="pm-h-81"></a>
#### Input regularity on the physical initial slice

The physical initial slice $\tau=0$ is the spacelike plane $y=-t$. We verify the full regularity family on this plane, including the nonround tests. After a kernel truncation uniform over all rows, let $E\subset K$ comprise the physical initial points joined to a test by retained kernel pairs. Equation <a href="#eq:phys-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-energy">[eq:phys-energy]</a> then bounds the test’s row mass by $CB^2|E|$, up to an error negligible relative to $\lVert g\rVert_2^2$. We therefore need a uniform kernel-localization estimate and a bound for $|E|$ by the test weight $r^4f^{1-\eta}$, allowing an arbitrarily small power loss.

<a id="stmt-lem-phys-initial-kernel"></a>
<div id="lem:phys-initial-kernel" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:phys-predecessor-relation"></a>
**Lemma 121** (Uniform packet localization from the initial slice). *Fix $\gamma_0>0$ and put $\Lambda=H^{-\gamma_0}$. The operator $g\mapsto V_1v(T)$ can be truncated to the following relation between an input point $z=(z_\perp,z_3)\in K$ and a row $(A,b,y)$: $$\begin{aligned}
 |b-z_\perp-(T-z_3)A|&\le C\Lambda\sqrt H,\notag\\
 |y+z_3-(T-z_3)|A|^2
       -2A\cdot(b-z_\perp-(T-z_3)A)|&\le C\Lambda H.
 \label{eq:phys-predecessor-relation}
\end{aligned}$$ For every $N$, the discarded operator has norm at most $C_NH^N$ from $L^2(K)$ to the row space. The constant is independent of any regularity test subsequently imposed on the output rows. The kernel vanishes unless $|A|\le A_0+C_\psi\sqrt H$, where $C_\psi$ is a radius containing the support of the fixed angular window $\psi$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-phys-initial-kernel"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-phys-initial-kernel</summary>

*Proof.* Insert the Fourier representation of $\widehat g$ into Equation <a href="#eq:phys-round-state" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-round-state">[eq:phys-round-state]</a> and the plateau analysis. The kernel has phase $$(b-z_\perp)\cdot\eta-(y+z_3)\rho
                  -(T-z_3)\frac{|\eta|^2}{4\rho}.$$ Its amplitude is supported in $H\rho\asymp1$ and $|\eta/(2\rho)-A|\le C_\psi\sqrt H$. Together with $|\eta/(2\rho)|\le A_0$ from Equation <a href="#eq:phys-patch" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-patch">[eq:phys-patch]</a>, this proves the stated angular support bound. On making the substitutions $\eta=2\rho A+H^{-1/2}\omega$ and $\sigma=H\rho$, the frequency Jacobian is $H^{-2}$, and the amplitude has uniformly bounded derivatives on a fixed compact set. The quadratic remainder in the phase also has bounded derivatives, because $T-z_3$ is bounded. Fourier integration by parts therefore gives $$|\mathcal K_T(A,b,y;z)|\le C_L H^{-2}
 \left(1+\frac{|\Delta b|}{\sqrt H}
              +\frac{|\Delta y|}{H}\right)^{-L},$$ where $\Delta b$ and $\Delta y$ are the two differences in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-predecessor-relation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-predecessor-relation">[eq:phys-predecessor-relation]</a>. Only bounded $A$ occur. The row measure at length $1$ is $H^{-1}\,dA\,db\,dy$. For fixed $A,z$, integration in $(b,y)$ costs the packet volume $H^2$. Squaring the kernel and then integrating over all rows and $z\in K$ thus gives a Hilbert–Schmidt bound of size at most a fixed power of $H^{-1}$. Outside the displayed relation, the decay factor adds an arbitrarily large inverse power of $\Lambda$. Since $\gamma_0$ is fixed, taking $L$ sufficiently large proves any prescribed $H^N$ bound. This estimate was made over all output rows, which proves the asserted uniformity. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-phys-predecessor-volume"></a>
<div id="lem:phys-predecessor-volume" class="lemma">

**Lemma 122** (Volume of physical predecessors). *Fix $0<\eta<1$. Consider any round-cone regularity test at time $T$ and length $1$, of angular width $r$ and relative thickness $f$, where $0<f\le1$ and $rf\ge\sqrt H$; for a round test set $f=1$. Let $E$ be the set of $z\in K$ related by Equation <a href="#eq:phys-predecessor-relation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-predecessor-relation">[eq:phys-predecessor-relation]</a> to some row of the test whose angular coordinate satisfies $|A|\le A_0+C_\psi\sqrt H$. There is a fixed $C_1$ such that <a id="eq:phys-predecessor-volume"></a>$$|E|\le C\Lambda^{C_1}r^4 f^{1-\eta}.
 \label{eq:phys-predecessor-volume}$$ The estimate is uniform in the center, $r$, and $f$ of the test.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-phys-predecessor-volume"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-phys-predecessor-volume</summary>

<a id="eq:phys-residuals"></a>
*Proof.* Use its normalized coordinates $$u=t-T,\quad x=\frac{b-b_*-uA_*}{r},\quad
 w=\frac{y-y_*-2A_*\cdot(b-b_*)+u|A_*|^2}{r^2},\quad
 V=\frac{A-A_*}{r}.$$ At $u=0$, the test has $|x|,|w|,|V|\le1$. The prediction at $T$ from a compatible input point differs from its tested row by $$|\delta x|\le C\Lambda\frac{\sqrt H}{r}\le C\Lambda f,
 \qquad
 |\delta w|\le C\Lambda\left(\frac H{r^2}
                      +|V|\frac{\sqrt H}{r}\right)
                  \le C\Lambda f.$$ Backflow to $t=z_3$ has bounded duration. Consequently the compatible normalized coordinates are bounded by a fixed power of $\Lambda$. For a nonround test, write its polynomial as $$F=c+du+\alpha\cdot x+\beta w+k(uw-|x|^2),\qquad
 G=F_u+V\cdot F_x+|V|^2F_w.$$ The coefficients are bounded, their discriminant is $1$, $G$ is constant on rays, and $F$ is affine on rays. Expanding at the tested row and then backflowing shows that, at a compatible input point, $$|F|+|G|\le C\Lambda^{C_2}f.
 \label{eq:phys-residuals}$$ Here and below the exponents of $\Lambda$ are fixed geometric constants.

<a id="eq:phys-input-plane"></a>
<a id="eq:phys-slice-jacobian"></a>
On the physical input plane the normalized variables satisfy $$(1+|A_*|^2)u=-T-y_*-2rA_*\cdot x-r^2w.
 \label{eq:phys-input-plane}$$ The absolute Jacobian of $(x,w)\mapsto(z_\perp,z_3)$ is $$\frac{r^4}{1+|A_*|^2}.
 \label{eq:phys-slice-jacobian}$$ Indeed $z_3=T+u$ and $z_\perp=b_*+uA_*+rx$; subtracting $A_*$ times the last row from the first two rows of their derivative matrix leaves determinant $r^2\partial_wu$. The crude volume of the bounded normalized box proves the lemma for round tests. It also proves it whenever $f$ is larger than a sufficiently small fixed inverse power of $\Lambda$.

<a id="eq:phys-gradient-identity"></a>
<a id="eq:phys-restricted-gradient"></a>
For the remaining $f$, the normalized coordinates are bounded by constants, and Equation <a href="#eq:phys-residuals" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-residuals">[eq:phys-residuals]</a> is as small as needed. The discriminant identity reads $$|F_x+2VF_w|^2=1+4(\beta+ku)G-4kF.
 \label{eq:phys-gradient-identity}$$ It implies $|F_x+2VF_w|\ge1/2$. Let $h(x,w)$ be the restriction of $F$ to Equation <a href="#eq:phys-input-plane" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-input-plane">[eq:phys-input-plane]</a>. Put $$a=\frac{2rA_*}{1+|A_*|^2},\qquad
 c_* =\frac{r^2}{1+|A_*|^2}.$$ Then $h_x=F_x-aF_u$, $h_w=F_w-c_*F_u$, and $$G=\frac{1+|A_*+rV|^2}{1+|A_*|^2}F_u
               +V\cdot h_x+|V|^2h_w.
 \label{eq:phys-restricted-gradient}$$ If $r$ is bounded by a fixed constant, a nonempty compatible set has bounded $A_*$, because its actual row velocities $A=A_*+rV$ are bounded. The coefficient of $F_u$ in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-restricted-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-restricted-gradient">[eq:phys-restricted-gradient]</a> is then bounded below. Together with Equation <a href="#eq:phys-gradient-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-gradient-identity">[eq:phys-gradient-identity]</a>, this gives $|\nabla h|\ge c>0$ once $|G|$ is sufficiently small.

For large $r$, replace the angular center by $0$. This is a boost of size $A_*/r$ in normalized coordinates; that size is bounded because $|A_*|\le r+A_0+C_\psi$. The boost preserves the discriminant and changes all bounded coordinates and coefficients by bounded amounts. Now $|V|\le C/r$, while $|F_w|=|\beta+ku|\le C$. Equation <a href="#eq:phys-gradient-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-gradient-identity">[eq:phys-gradient-identity]</a> gives $|F_x|\ge1/4$ for all sufficiently large $r$. In these coordinates $u$ in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-input-plane" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-input-plane">[eq:phys-input-plane]</a> is independent of $x$, so $h_x=F_x$. Choosing the cutoff between the two ranges once and for all proves a uniform lower bound for the restricted gradient.

The polynomial $h$ has degree at most two. In a fixed bounded box, the set $\{|h|\le q,\ |\nabla h|\ge c\}$ has volume at most $Cq$, uniformly in its coefficients: partition according to a coordinate derivative of magnitude at least $c/\sqrt3$, hold the other coordinates fixed, and split the one-dimensional fiber at the zeros of that derivative. There are at most two monotonic pieces, on each of which the mean value theorem gives length $O(q)$. Applying this with $q=C\Lambda^{C_2}f$, and then using Equation <a href="#eq:phys-slice-jacobian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-slice-jacobian">[eq:phys-slice-jacobian]</a> (or $r^4$ after recentering), gives $|E|\le C\Lambda^{C_3}r^4f$ in the small-$f$ case. Since $f\le f^{1-\eta}$, this suffices. In the complementary case the missing factor $f^{1-\eta}$ costs only another fixed power of $\Lambda$, as already noted. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prop-phys-input-regularity"></a>
<div id="prop:phys-input-regularity" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:phys-kappa"></a>
**Proposition 123** (Regularity of the initial analyzed state). *Fix $0<\eta<1$ as in Definition <a href="#rt:regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rt:regularity">91</a>. For every $\gamma>0$, the state in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-round-state" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-round-state">[eq:phys-round-state]</a> has input regularity constant $$\kappa=C_{\eta,\gamma}H^{-\gamma}B^2
 \label{eq:phys-kappa}$$ at each of the bounded starting times $T$. Under Equation <a href="#eq:phys-energy-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-energy-range">[eq:phys-energy-range]</a>, it also satisfies the polynomial-size and negligible-tail hypotheses of the round-wave experiment with terminal length $s=H$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-phys-input-regularity"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-phys-input-regularity</summary>

*Proof.* Choose $\gamma_0>0$ so small that $C_1\gamma_0<\gamma/2$ in Lemma <a href="#lem:phys-predecessor-volume" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:phys-predecessor-volume">122</a>. For a test $\mathcal T$, restrict $g$ to its predecessor set $E$. The truncated operator of Lemma <a href="#lem:phys-initial-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:phys-initial-kernel">121</a> sends $g\mathbf1_{K\setminus E}$ to zero on $\mathcal T$. The unrestricted operator on $g\mathbf1_E$ has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm by Equation <a href="#eq:phys-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-energy">[eq:phys-energy]</a>. Thus, for every $N$, $$\mu_T(\mathcal T)
 \le C\lVert g\mathbf 1_E\rVert_2^2+C_NH^N\lVert g\rVert_2^2
 \le C B^2H^{-C_1\gamma_0}r^4f^{1-\eta}+C_NH^N B^2.$$ The uncertainty condition gives the uniform weight floor <a id="eq:phys-weight-floor"></a>$$r^4f^{1-\eta}=(rf)^4f^{-3-\eta}\ge H^2.
 \label{eq:phys-weight-floor}$$ Taking $N$ large proves regularity with Equation <a href="#eq:phys-kappa" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-kappa">[eq:phys-kappa]</a>, including every admissible width.

The ratios $e/\kappa$ and $\kappa/e$ are bounded above by fixed powers of $H^{-1}$ by Equation <a href="#eq:phys-energy-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-energy-range">[eq:phys-energy-range]</a>. The kernel proof gives negligible phase tails outside a fixed polynomial box: the input is compact, all velocities and durations are bounded, and arbitrary decay is available. Its pointwise kernel bound also gives a phase-density bound by a fixed power of $H^{-1}$ times $B^2$, and hence times $e$. All these estimates are uniform along any sequence of the present inputs. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-82"></a>
#### Recovering the physical norm from leaf masses

<a id="stmt-lem-phys-synthesis"></a>
<div id="lem:phys-synthesis" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:phys-synthesis"></a>
**Lemma 124** (Synthesis at the terminal scale). *Let $v$ be the wave in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-round-state" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-round-state">[eq:phys-round-state]</a>, and let $\Omega$ be a fixed bounded subset of $(b,y)$ space. At each left endpoint $T_j=T+jH$ in $[T,T+1]$, use a plateau analysis of length $H$, and group its row masses into spatial $H$-grid cubes. Restrict to a fixed enlargement of $\Omega$, and denote the resulting masses by $m_{j,Q}$. They are admissible round-test assignments with weights bounded above and below by positive constants. For every $0<\sigma<1$ and $N$, $$\int_T^{T+1}\int_\Omega |v|^3
 \le C_\sigma H^{-C_4\sigma}H^{-1/2}
                 \sum_{j,Q}m_{j,Q}^{3/2}
       +C_{N,\sigma}H^N e^{3/2}.
 \label{eq:phys-synthesis}$$ Here $H$ is dyadic, so the time partition is exact.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-phys-synthesis"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-phys-synthesis</summary>

*Proof.* At length $H$, the angular aperture is $d_H=1$ and both spatial packet widths are $H$. All row angles lie in a fixed bounded set. A fixed round test with $r\ge1$, centered at a given cube, contains that cube and all these angles. Its weight $r^4$ is a fixed constant, and different cube assignments are disjoint in row space.

Synthesize the plateau analysis and propagate for $0\le h\le H$. The same frequency calculation as in Lemma <a href="#lem:phys-initial-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:phys-initial-kernel">121</a>, now with frequency boxes of volume $O(H^{-3})$, gives a kernel bounded by $$C_L H^{-3}\left(1+
       \frac{|(b,y)-(b',y')|}{H}\right)^{-L}.$$ The bounded ray displacement during $h$ is $O(H)$ and has been absorbed in this bound. Its squared integral over source rows is $O(H^{-3})$. For an output point in a cube $Q$, retain only rows in cubes within distance $C H^{1-\sigma}$ of $Q$. Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds the retained contribution by $$C H^{-3/2}
 \left(\sum_{Q'\sim Q}m_{j,Q'}\right)^{1/2}.$$ The omitted contribution is at most $C_{N,\sigma}H^N\sqrt e$ pointwise, by arbitrary kernel decay. For $H$ sufficiently small, all retained cubes lie in the chosen fixed enlargement of $\Omega$. There are $O(H^{-3\sigma})$ neighbors of any $Q$, with the same bound on overlap. The spacetime cell over $Q$ has volume $H^4$. Cubing the pointwise estimate, integrating over that cell, and using $$\left(\sum_{Q'\sim Q}m_{j,Q'}\right)^{3/2}
 \le \#\{Q'\sim Q\}^{1/2}
              \sum_{Q'\sim Q}m_{j,Q'}^{3/2}$$ proves Equation <a href="#eq:phys-synthesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-synthesis">[eq:phys-synthesis]</a>; for example, any fixed $C_4\ge5$ suffices after harmless enlargement. There are only $O(H^{-4})$ spacetime cells, and arbitrary decay absorbs their number in the error term. ◻

</details>

<a id="eq:phys-round-application"></a>
We explain explicitly how to use the exponent formulation of Theorem <a href="#thm:round" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:round">104</a>. Its wave bound, with regularity parameter $\eta$, is $\Gamma_{\mathrm{wav},\mathrm{round}}\le100\eta$. Hence for the uniform class of experiments constructed above and every $\zeta>0$, $$H^{-1/2}\sum_{j,Q}m_{j,Q}^{3/2}
 \le C_{\eta,\gamma,\zeta}H^{-100\eta-\zeta}e\sqrt\kappa.
 \label{eq:phys-round-application}$$ The bounded weights have been absorbed into the constant. For completeness, at each fixed $H$ the normalized functional is at most $C H^{-3/2}\sqrt{e/\kappa}\le C H^{-3/2}$: there are $H^{-1}$ cuts and each has total assigned mass at most $e$. Thus, if no constant in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-round-application" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-round-application">[eq:phys-round-application]</a> existed, there would be a sequence $H\downarrow0$ along which the normalized functional exceeds $H^{-100\eta-\zeta}$. The regularity and tail estimates of Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-input-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-input-regularity">123</a> give one admissible polynomial sequence with all fixed setup constants uniform. Its upper growth exponent would be at least $100\eta+\zeta$, contrary to Theorem <a href="#thm:round" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:round">104</a>.

<a id="eq:phys-level-estimate"></a>
Combining Equations <a href="#eq:phys-synthesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-synthesis">[eq:phys-synthesis]</a>, <a href="#eq:phys-round-application" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-round-application">[eq:phys-round-application]</a>, and <a href="#eq:phys-kappa" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-kappa">[eq:phys-kappa]</a> gives $$\int_T^{T+1}\int_\Omega |v|^3
 \le C H^{-100\eta-\zeta-\gamma/2-C_4\sigma}
                    B\lVert g\rVert_2^2.
 \label{eq:phys-level-estimate}$$ The error term is absorbed here using $e^{3/2}\le C B\lVert g\rVert_2^2$. The small-energy case was already handled in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-small-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-small-energy">[eq:phys-small-energy]</a>. Given any $\beta>0$, first take $100\eta<\beta/4$, then $\zeta<\beta/4$, $\gamma/2<\beta/4$, and $C_4\sigma<\beta/4$; finally choose $\gamma_0$ as in Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-input-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-input-regularity">123</a>. Thus the loss in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-level-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-level-estimate">[eq:phys-level-estimate]</a> is smaller than any prescribed $\beta$. The finitely many null-time intervals and the constant Jacobian in Equation <a href="#eq:phys-null-coordinates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-null-coordinates">[eq:phys-null-coordinates]</a> do not change this conclusion.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-phys-synthesis-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-phys-synthesis</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-annular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-annular">120</a>.* It remains to pass from bounded amplitude pieces to arbitrary localized input. Normalize $\lVert g\rVert_3=1$ with $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}g\subset K$. Fix an integer $M>4$. The parts where $|g|<H^M$ and where $|g|>H^{-M}$ have $L^1$ norms at most $|K|H^M$ and $H^{2M}$, respectively. The elementary bound $\lVert K_{H,\tau}\rVert_\infty\le C H^{-3}$ shows that their contributions on the bounded output region are uniformly bounded, indeed tend to zero. No frequency restriction has been applied to $g$ before making these spatial and amplitude restrictions.

Split the remaining part into disjoint dyadic amplitude pieces $g_\nu$. Their number is $L=O_M(1+\log H^{-1})$, and, with $B_\nu=\lVert g_\nu\rVert_\infty$, $$B_\nu\lVert g_\nu\rVert_2^2\le2\lVert g_\nu\rVert_3^3,
 \qquad \sum_\nu\lVert g_\nu\rVert_3^3\le1.$$ Equation <a href="#eq:phys-level-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-level-estimate">[eq:phys-level-estimate]</a>, with parameters making its exponent less than $\delta$, and the inequality $$\lVert \sum_{\nu=1}^L h_\nu\rVert_3^3
 \le L^2\sum_\nu\lVert h_\nu\rVert_3^3$$ give the local cubed bound $C L^2H^{-\delta}$. Since $L^2\le C_\delta H^{-\delta}$, taking a cube root yields a loss at most $H^{-2\delta/3}\le H^{-\delta}$. Homogeneity removes the normalization. Sum the cubed estimates over the output cubes, using the bounded overlap of their enlarged input cubes and Equation <a href="#eq:phys-far-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-far-kernel">[eq:phys-far-kernel]</a>. Finally sum the fixed angular partition. This proves Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-annular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-annular">120</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-83"></a>
#### Sobolev summation and the remaining exponents

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-phys-synthesis-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-phys-synthesis</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.* Let $h=J^\varepsilon f$. Use a smooth radial partition into a low-frequency cutoff and annuli $|\xi|\asymp2^n$, $n\ge0$. On the $n$th annulus put the multiplier $J^{-\varepsilon}$ into $a_H$, where $H=2^{-n}$. After factoring out $H^\varepsilon$, the rescaled symbols have uniformly bounded derivatives. Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-annular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-annular">120</a>, applied with $\delta=\varepsilon/2$, gives $$\lVert W(P_nJ^{-\varepsilon}h)\rVert_{L^3_{x,\tau}(\mathbb R^3\times[1,2])}
 \le C_\varepsilon 2^{-n\varepsilon/2}\lVert h\rVert_3.$$ The series is summable by the triangle inequality.

We also record a direct justification at frequency zero. For a smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $|\xi|\le2$, decompose $$\chi(\xi)e^{-i\tau|\xi|}
 =\chi(\xi)+\chi(\xi)(e^{-i\tau|\xi|}-1).$$ The first term has an integrable convolution kernel. Split the second into annuli of radius $\lambda=2^{-j}\le1$. In variables $\xi=\lambda\omega$, its symbol and its derivatives through order $4$ are $O(\lambda)$ on a fixed annulus, uniformly for $1\le\tau\le2$. Integration by parts using $(1-\Delta_\omega)^2$ shows that its inverse Fourier transform has $L^1$ norm $O(\lambda)$. These norms sum. The smooth low-frequency factor $J^{-\varepsilon}$ preserves the same bounds. Young’s inequality therefore handles the low-frequency term. The resulting inequality is exactly the negative-sign version of Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>; complex conjugation proves the stated sign. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-cor-full-range"></a>
<div id="cor:full-range" class="corollary">

<a id="eq:phys-full-range"></a>
**Corollary 125** (The positive-regularity local-smoothing range). *For every $2<p<\infty$ and $\alpha>\max\{0,1-3/p\}$, $$\lVert Uf\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3\times[1,2])}
 \le C_{p,\alpha}\lVert J^\alpha f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \qquad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)).
 \label{eq:phys-full-range}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-full-range"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-full-range</summary>

<a id="eq:phys-infinity-bound"></a>
*Proof.* Take a smooth radial annular cutoff $P_\lambda=\phi(|D|/\lambda)$, $\lambda\ge1$. Plancherel gives $$\lVert UP_\lambda\rVert_{L^2_x\to L^2_{x,\tau}}\le C,$$ and Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-annular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-annular">120</a> gives, for every $\delta>0$, $\lVert UP_\lambda\rVert_{L^3_x\to L^3_{x,\tau}}\le C_\delta\lambda^\delta$. We first prove the remaining endpoint bound $$\lVert UP_\lambda\rVert_{L^\infty_x\to L^\infty_{x,\tau}}
 \le C\lambda.
 \label{eq:phys-infinity-bound}$$ The radial kernel, at $r=|x|>0$, is a fixed constant times $$\frac1r\int_0^\infty e^{i\tau\rho}
             \rho\phi(\rho/\lambda)\sin(r\rho)\,d\rho.$$ Put $I(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{is\rho}\rho\phi(\rho/\lambda)\,d\rho$. For every $N$, $$|I(s)|\le C_N\lambda^2(1+\lambda|s|)^{-N},\qquad
 |I'(s)|\le C_N\lambda^3(1+\lambda|s|)^{-N}.$$ The kernel is a constant times $r^{-1}(I(\tau+r)-I(\tau-r))$. If $0<r\le1/2$, the mean value theorem and $1\le\tau\le2$ bound it by $C_N\lambda^{3-N}$, which also removes the apparent singularity at $r=0$. If $r\ge1/2$, its absolute value is at most $$C_N\frac{\lambda^2}{r}
 \big((1+\lambda|\tau-r|)^{-N}
                +(1+\lambda(\tau+r))^{-N}\big).$$ Multiplying by $r^2$ and integrating in $r$ gives $C\lambda$: the first summand uses $\int_{1/2}^\infty r(1+\lambda|\tau-r|)^{-N}\,dr\le C/\lambda$, and the second is smaller. Hence the kernel has $L^1$ norm at most $C\lambda$, proving Equation <a href="#eq:phys-infinity-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-infinity-bound">[eq:phys-infinity-bound]</a>.

Interpolation between the $L^2$ and $L^3$ estimates gives an arbitrarily small positive power of $\lambda$ for every $2<p\le3$. For $p>3$, interpolate the $L^3$ bound with Equation <a href="#eq:phys-infinity-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-infinity-bound">[eq:phys-infinity-bound]</a>; the $L^3$ interpolation weight is $3/p$, giving $$\lVert UP_\lambda\rVert_{L^p_x\to L^p_{x,\tau}}
 \le C_{p,\delta}\lambda^{1-3/p+3\delta/p}.$$ Choose $\delta$ small enough that this exponent, or its counterpart for $p\le3$, is strictly below $\alpha$. The same estimates hold for uniformly smooth radial annular symbol families, as both the kernel proof and Proposition <a href="#prop:phys-annular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:phys-annular">120</a> are uniform for those families. We may thus insert $J^{-\alpha}$ into each annular symbol, factor out $\lambda^{-\alpha}$, and sum the resulting geometric series. The low-frequency kernels have uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms by the preceding proof, which applies to every $L^p$. This proves Equation <a href="#eq:phys-full-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:phys-full-range">[eq:phys-full-range]</a>. ◻

</details>

The same estimate describes the wave equation with independent initial displacement $u_0$ and velocity $u_1$. For Schwartz data its solution is $$u(t)=\cos(t|D|)u_0+\frac{\sin(t|D|)}{|D|}u_1,$$ and for the exponents in Corollary <a href="#cor:full-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:full-range">125</a>, $$\lVert u\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3\times[1,2])}
 \le C_{p,\alpha}
 \bigl(\lVert J^\alpha u_0\rVert_p+\lVert J^{\alpha-1}u_1\rVert_p\bigr).$$ At high frequency this follows from the two signs of the half-wave estimate and the order $-1$ velocity multiplier. At low frequency, retain the combined multiplier $\sin(t|\xi|)/|\xi|$: it is smooth at zero and, after a smooth frequency cutoff, has a uniformly integrable kernel for $1\le t\le2$. Density extends the solution estimate to the indicated Sobolev data.

<a id="pm-h-84"></a>
#### Maximal half-waves and convergence to the initial data

The spacetime estimate also controls the largest value of the wave over a finite time interval, at the cost of additional regularity. This gives a pointwise interpretation of the evolution for Sobolev initial data. For $s\in\mathbb R$ and $1<p<\infty$, write $W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^3)=\{f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3):J^s f\in L^p(\mathbb R^3)\}$, with norm $\lVert J^s f\rVert_p$.

<a id="stmt-cor-wave-maximal"></a>
<div id="cor:wave-maximal" class="corollary">

<a id="eq:wave-maximal"></a>
<a id="eq:wave-initial-limit"></a>
**Corollary 126** (Maximal half-wave and pointwise convergence). *Let $3\le p<\infty$ and $s>1-2/p$. Then $$\label{eq:wave-maximal}
 \left\|\sup_{0<t<1}|Uf(\cdot,t)|\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \le C_{p,s}\lVert J^s f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \qquad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)).$$ The family has a bounded maximal extension to $W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^3)$, and in that extension every $f\in W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $$\label{eq:wave-initial-limit}
 \lim_{t\downarrow0}Uf(x,t)=f(x)
 \quad\text{for almost every }x\in\mathbb R^3.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-wave-maximal"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-wave-maximal</summary>

*Proof.* For $p\ge3$, Corollary <a href="#cor:full-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:full-range">125</a> gives the $1/p-$ local smoothing gain relative to the fixed-time loss $1-2/p$. The established maximal implication (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2019, sec. 3.5, Equation (3.24)) <a id="pm-cite-34"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey)] therefore gives <a href="#eq:wave-maximal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wave-maximal">[eq:wave-maximal]</a>. At each frequency, Sobolev embedding in time costs arbitrarily more than $1/p$ derivatives; together with local smoothing, this requires regularity arbitrarily close to $1-2/p$ from above. The strict inequality on $s$ absorbs the remaining positive losses. The implication uses scaling to cover the time intervals approaching zero.

For Schwartz data, the Fourier integral converges uniformly to the initial data as $t\downarrow0$. Schwartz functions are dense in $W^{s,p}$, and the maximal bound gives the extension and carries this convergence to every such datum. More explicitly, for a Schwartz approximation $g$ to $f$, the measure of the set where $\limsup_{t\downarrow0}|Uf-f|>\eta$ is at most $C_{p,s}\eta^{-p}\lVert J^s(f-g)\rVert_p^p$. Letting $g\to f$ proves <a href="#eq:wave-initial-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:wave-initial-limit">[eq:wave-initial-limit]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:bochner-riesz"></a>
### Bochner–Riesz consequences

We apply the established local-smoothing implications of Beltran–Hickman–Sogge to Corollary <a href="#cor:full-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:full-range">125</a>. The maximal result concerns the family in <a href="#eq:intro-br-means" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:intro-br-means">[eq:intro-br-means]</a>; the subsequent nonmaximal result concerns the individual linear means. These means recover a function by gradually admitting higher frequencies, with order $\delta$ smoothing the boundary of the Fourier ball. Uniform $L^p$ bounds make each approximation stable. A maximal bound is stronger: it controls the error for all radii at once, which allows the elementary convergence for Schwartz data to pass to every $L^p$ datum by density.

For $p\ge3$, the local-smoothing input has an arbitrarily small positive loss beyond $1-3/p$. The strict inequality $\delta>1-3/p$ absorbs that loss in the established implication. Thus the conclusion below requires only $L^p$ integrability of the data, in contrast to the Sobolev hypothesis in the maximal half-wave corollary.

<a id="stmt-thm-br-maximal"></a>
<div id="thm:br-maximal" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:br-maximal"></a>
<a id="eq:br-ae"></a>
**Theorem 127** (Maximal Bochner–Riesz bounds and almost-everywhere summation). *Let $3\le p<\infty$ and $\delta>1-3/p$. Then $$\label{eq:br-maximal}
 \lVert B_*^\delta f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \le C_{p,\delta}\lVert f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \qquad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)).$$ The family has a bounded maximal extension to $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$, and in that extension every $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $$\label{eq:br-ae}
 \lim_{R\to\infty}B_R^\delta f(x)=f(x)
 \quad\text{for almost every }x\in\mathbb R^3.$$ In particular, every $\delta>0$ is allowed when $p=3$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-br-maximal"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-br-maximal</summary>

*Proof.* For $p\ge3$, the sharp fixed-time Sobolev loss is $1-2/p$. Corollary <a href="#cor:full-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:full-range">125</a> permits every exponent $\alpha=1-3/p+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon>0$, and hence gives the $1/p-$ local smoothing hypothesis for the Euclidean half-wave in (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2019, Proposition 3.3) <a id="pm-cite-35"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey)]. That proposition applies for $2n/(n-1)\le p<\infty$ and order above $$\max\left\{n\left|\frac1p-\frac12\right|-\frac12,0\right\}.$$ For $n=3$ and $p\ge3$ this threshold is $1-3/p$. The arbitrary positive loss in the local-smoothing input is absorbed by the strict inequality on $\delta$.

The cited proposition uses the multiplier $(1-t|\xi|)_+^\delta$. Write $\mathcal L_R^\delta$ for the same means with $t=R^{-1}$ and $\mathcal L_*^\delta f=\sup_{R>0}|\mathcal L_R^\delta f|$. It gives the asserted strong bound for $\mathcal L_*^\delta$. Here is the transfer to the squared-radius convention in <a href="#eq:intro-br-means" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:intro-br-means">[eq:intro-br-means]</a>. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty))$ equal to one on a neighborhood of $[1/2,1]$, and put $$a(\xi)=\chi(|\xi|)(1+|\xi|)^\delta,\qquad
 b(\xi)=(1-\chi(|\xi|))(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta.$$ Both $a$ and $b$ are smooth and compactly supported on $\mathbb R^3$, and $$\left(1-\frac{|\xi|^2}{R^2}\right)_+^\delta
 =a(\xi/R)\left(1-\frac{|\xi|}{R}\right)_+^\delta+b(\xi/R).$$ The inverse Fourier transforms of $a$ and $b$ are Schwartz functions. Their dilates are bounded in absolute value by $C_N R^3(1+R|x|)^{-N}$ for any fixed $N>3$, so the Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator $\mathcal M$ gives the pointwise estimate $$B_*^\delta f
 \le C_\delta\bigl(\mathcal M(\mathcal L_*^\delta f)+\mathcal Mf\bigr).$$ Its $L^p$ boundedness for $p>1$ proves <a href="#eq:br-maximal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-maximal">[eq:br-maximal]</a>.

For $g\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, dominated convergence in the Fourier integral gives $B_R^\delta g\to g$ uniformly as $R\to\infty$. For $f\in L^p$, choose $g_j\in\mathcal S$ converging to $f$ in $L^p$ with $\sum_j\lVert g_{j+1}-g_j\rVert_p<\infty$. The maximal inequality places $\sum_j B_*^\delta(g_{j+1}-g_j)$ in $L^p$. Thus $B_R^\delta g_j$ converges uniformly in $R$ for almost every $x$, defining the usual maximal extension; for each fixed $R$ it agrees with the bounded $L^p$ extension of $B_R^\delta$. For $g\in\mathcal S$, $$\limsup_{R\to\infty}|B_R^\delta f-f|
 \le B_*^\delta(f-g)+|f-g|
 \quad\text{almost everywhere}.$$ Chebyshev’s inequality and <a href="#eq:br-maximal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-maximal">[eq:br-maximal]</a> bound the measure where this limsup exceeds $\eta>0$ by $C_{p,\delta}\eta^{-p}\lVert f-g\rVert_p^p$. Density then proves <a href="#eq:br-ae" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-ae">[eq:br-ae]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-cor-br-nonmaximal"></a>
<div id="cor:br-nonmaximal" class="corollary">

<a id="eq:br-nonmaximal"></a>
**Corollary 128** (The full strict nonmaximal range). *For $1\le p\le\infty$, with $1/\infty=0$, set $$\delta_{\mathrm{BR}}(p)
 =\max\left\{3\left|\frac1p-\frac12\right|-\frac12,0\right\}.$$ If $\delta>\delta_{\mathrm{BR}}(p)$, the operators $B_R^\delta$ extend boundedly to $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ with a bound uniform in $R>0$: $$\label{eq:br-nonmaximal}
 \lVert B_R^\delta f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}
 \le C_{p,\delta}\lVert f\rVert_{L^p(\mathbb R^3)}.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-br-nonmaximal"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-br-nonmaximal</summary>

*Proof.* Proposition 3.2 of (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2019) <a id="pm-cite-36"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey)], with the same local-smoothing input and the same smooth-factor transfer, gives <a href="#eq:br-nonmaximal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:br-nonmaximal">[eq:br-nonmaximal]</a> for $3\le p<\infty$ and $\delta>1-3/p$; dilation makes the constants uniform in $R$. For $2\le p\le3$, fix any $\delta>0$ and interpolate the $p=3$ bound at that order with the $L^2$ bound from Plancherel. This gives the required threshold $\delta_{\mathrm{BR}}(p)=0$ in this interval. The multiplier is real and even, so duality gives the range $1<p<2$, since $\delta_{\mathrm{BR}}(p)=\delta_{\mathrm{BR}}(p')$. Finally, at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ the stated condition is $\delta>1$. The inverse Fourier transform $K^\delta$ of $(1-|\xi|^2)_+^\delta$ obeys $|K^\delta(x)|\le C_\delta(1+|x|)^{-2-\delta}$ and is therefore integrable at these orders. Its dilates have the same $L^1$ norm, so Young’s inequality supplies both endpoint bounds. ◻

</details>

For $1\le p<\infty$ in this strict range, the uniform bounds also give $B_R^\delta f\to f$ in $L^p$ as $R\to\infty$. One first checks this for Schwartz functions with compact Fourier support and then uses their density in $L^p$ together with the uniform operator bound.

The interpolation and duality in this corollary apply to the fixed-radius linear operators; the maximal conclusion remains the range of Theorem <a href="#thm:br-maximal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:br-maximal">127</a>. For comparison, the separate article (OpenAI 2026, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 12.4) <a id="pm-cite-37"></a>[[OpenAIBochnerRiesz2026](#ref-OpenAIBochnerRiesz2026)] proves positive-order $L^3$ boundedness and the same strict nonmaximal range by a different argument. That article is not an input to the deduction above.

<a id="subsec:restriction-kakeya"></a>
#### Spherical restriction and Kakeya maximal estimates

<a id="eq:sphere-extension"></a>
The strict multiplier range has further established consequences for Fourier extension and tube geometry. Let $d\sigma$ be surface measure on $S^2$, and define the spherical extension operator by $$Eg(x)=\int_{S^2}e^{ix\cdot\omega}g(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega).$$ Tao’s Bochner–Riesz-to-restriction implication (Tao 1999) <a id="pm-cite-38"></a>[[Tao1999Restriction](#ref-Tao1999Restriction)], also described in (Beltran, Hickman, and Sogge 2019, sec. 3.1) <a id="pm-cite-39"></a>[[BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey](#ref-BeltranHickmanSogge2019Survey)], applies to Corollary <a href="#cor:br-nonmaximal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:br-nonmaximal">128</a>. By duality it gives $$\label{eq:sphere-extension}
 \lVert Eg\rVert_{L^r(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_r\lVert g\rVert_{L^r(S^2,d\sigma)},
 \qquad 3<r<\infty.$$ Thus the multiplier bounds also control the physical-space concentration of waves with Fourier support on the sphere. The strict family of positive-order Bochner–Riesz bounds supplies the premise; no order-zero multiplier assertion is needed.

For $0<h<1$ and $\omega\in S^2$, let $\mathcal T_h(\omega)$ be the family of all unit-length tubes of radius $h$ parallel to $\omega$, at arbitrary spatial positions, and put $$K_hF(\omega)=\sup_{T\in\mathcal T_h(\omega)}
              \frac1{|T|}\int_T|F(x)|\,dx.$$ The restriction-to-Kakeya implication of (Wolff 1999, sec. 4, Proposition 4.1) <a id="pm-cite-40"></a>[[Wolff1999Kakeya](#ref-Wolff1999Kakeya)] applies to the diagonal extension range <a href="#eq:sphere-extension" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sphere-extension">[eq:sphere-extension]</a>. For $r>3$ sufficiently close to $3$, it first gives restricted weak type $(a,a)$, where $a=r/(r-2)<3$, with norm $O(h^{-2(3/a-1)})$ for the tubes above. Interpolation with the trivial $L^\infty$ bound gives strong type $(3,3)$ with loss $h^{-2(1-a/3)}$. Since $a\uparrow3$ as $r\downarrow3$, this yields the Kakeya maximal estimate, for every $F\in L^3(\mathbb R^3)$, <a id="eq:kakeya-maximal"></a>$$\label{eq:kakeya-maximal}
 \lVert K_hF\rVert_{L^3(S^2,d\sigma)}
 \le C_\varepsilon h^{-\varepsilon}\lVert F\rVert_{L^3(\mathbb R^3)},
 \qquad \varepsilon>0,\quad 0<h<1.$$ This quantitatively controls averages over thin tubes in every direction. In particular, a compact set containing a unit line segment in each direction has Hausdorff dimension three. Wang–Zahl already proved the Hausdorff and Minkowski dimension assertions (Wang and Zahl 2025, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-41"></a>[[WangZahl2025Kakeya](#ref-WangZahl2025Kakeya)]; the maximal estimate is a stronger quantitative conclusion. The deductions here use the established Bochner–Riesz-to-restriction-to-Kakeya chain and also apply to the independent Bochner–Riesz result cited above.

      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[\n node distance=7mm and 9mm,\n every node/.style={font=\\small,align=center},\n result/.style={draw,inner sep=6pt,text width=43mm},\n >={Stealth[length=2mm]}]\n \\node[result] (inputs) {Planar incidences\\\\Lower-dimensional waves};\n \\node[result,right=of inputs] (cylinder) {Cylindrical packet estimates\\\\Theorem~\\ref{thm:cylinder}};\n \\node[result,below=of cylinder] (transfer) {Thin round tests\\\\Transfer to the cylinder};\n \\node[result,left=of transfer] (round) {Round-cone estimates\\\\Theorem~\\ref{thm:round}};\n \\node[result,below=of round] (physical) {Physical input regularity\\\\Theorem~\\ref{thm:main}};\n \\draw[->] (inputs)--(cylinder);\n \\draw[->] (cylinder)--(transfer);\n \\draw[->] (transfer)--(round);\n \\draw[->] (inputs)--(round);\n \\draw[->] (round)--(physical);\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "A dependency flowchart consisting of five rectangular boxes connected by directed arrows:\n- Top-left box contains:\n  \"Planar incidences\"\n  \"Lower-dimensional waves\"\n- Top-right box contains:\n  \"Cylindrical\"\n  \"packet estimates\"\n  \"Theorem 3.6\"\n- Middle-right box contains:\n  \"Thin round tests\"\n  \"Transfer to the cylinder\"\n- Middle-left box contains:\n  \"Round-cone estimates\"\n  \"Theorem 9.1\"\n- Bottom box (centered below the middle-left box) contains:\n  \"Physical input regularity\"\n  \"Theorem 1.1\"\n\nArrows between boxes:\n- A horizontal arrow points from the right side of \"Planar incidences / Lower-dimensional waves\" to the left side of \"Cylindrical / packet estimates / Theorem 3.6\".\n- A vertical arrow points downwards from the bottom of \"Cylindrical / packet estimates / Theorem 3.6\" to the top of \"Thin round tests / Transfer to the cylinder\".\n- A horizontal arrow points from the left side of \"Thin round tests / Transfer to the cylinder\" to the right side of \"Round-cone estimates / Theorem 9.1\".\n- A vertical arrow points downwards from the bottom of \"Round-cone estimates / Theorem 9.1\" to the top of \"Physical input regularity / Theorem 1.1\"."
    }
